The figure illustrates a human parsing pipeline composed of four main stages: Segment Generation, Segment Feature Extraction, Segment Ranking and Selection, and Part Assembling by And-or Graph. The global layout is left-to-right, with data flowing from an input image of a person on the far left through successive processing modules to produce a segmented human body map on the far right. The input image is processed in two parallel streams: one for segment generation using image segmentation techniques, and another for pose estimation, which provides skeletal keypoints used for pose-based feature extraction.

In the Segment Generation module, the input image is divided into multiple candidate segments, visually represented as small, irregularly shaped regions (e.g., parts of clothing or body limbs), shown in grayscale with blue outlines. These segments are then passed to the Segment Feature Extraction module, where three types of features are computed for each segment: traditional appearance features (represented by vertical bars with black stripes), deep-learned features (vertical bars with pink stripes), and pose-based features (vertical bars with orange stripes). The pose-based features are derived from a separate stream that first estimates the human pose (shown as a stick figure overlaid on the input image with colored joints and limbs) and then extracts features based on spatial relationships between the segments and the pose keypoints.

The extracted features are then used in the Segment Ranking and Selection module. Here, segments are ranked and selected based on their feature quality; top-ranked segments are enclosed in red dashed boxes, while lower-ranked ones are in gray dashed boxes. A purple downward arrow indicates the selection process, filtering out less relevant segments.

The selected segments are then fed into the Part Assembling by And-or Graph module. This module uses a hierarchical graph structure to assemble the final human parsing result. At the top, a 'human' node branches into 'human configuration 1' and other configurations. Each configuration decomposes into upper-body and lower-body components, which further break down into specific parts like head & torso, left arm, right arm, etc. For each part, multiple candidate segments (represented by geometric shapes like stars, triangles, and circles in various colors) are considered. The graph structure allows for flexible assembly via AND (all required parts) and OR (any one of several candidates) logic. The final assembled result is a color-coded human body segmentation map, where different body parts are labeled with distinct colors (e.g., blue for hair, green for upper clothes, yellow for lower clothes, etc.), as indicated in the legend at the bottom right. Dashed lines connect the selected segments back to the graph, showing how they are assigned to specific body parts. The entire pipeline is designed to progressively refine and assemble a coherent human parsing output from raw image data.

The figure presents two side-by-side diagrams, labeled (a) and (b), illustrating the application of a proposed method in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) using stacked 'quasi-hexagonal' kernels. Both diagrams depict a three-layered CNN structure, with layers labeled as Layer l, Layer l+1, and Layer l+2, arranged vertically from bottom to top. Each layer is represented as a grid of square units, symbolizing feature maps or activation maps, with multiple such grids stacked horizontally to indicate depth or channels.

In diagram (a), the kernel pattern used in Layer l is labeled 'L' and is visually represented by a green rectangular region within the grid, surrounded by an orange border indicating the receptive field. In Layer l+1, the kernel pattern is labeled 'U', shown as a blue rectangular region. The output neuron N(i,j,c) in Layer l+2 is highlighted in red, and arrows connect it to the corresponding receptive fields across the layers, demonstrating the convolution operation followed by non-linearity. The receptive fields for the neuron are explicitly labeled and span across all three layers, showing how the kernel patterns stack to form the final receptive field.

Diagram (b) mirrors the structure of (a) but swaps the kernel patterns between layers: Layer l uses kernel pattern 'U' (blue region), while Layer l+1 uses kernel pattern 'L' (green region). Despite this reversal, the resulting receptive field for the neuron N(i,j,c) in Layer l+2 remains identical in shape and extent to that in (a), as indicated by the consistent red highlight and connecting arrows. This demonstrates that the final receptive field pattern is invariant to the order of kernel application, provided the same set of kernel patterns is used across the layers.

Both diagrams include labels for 'convolution + non-linearity' pointing to the connections between layers, emphasizing the standard CNN processing steps. The kernel patterns 'L' and 'U' are visually distinct in color (green and blue respectively) and are positioned centrally within each layer’s grid. The receptive fields are outlined with black lines and shaded in orange, clearly demarcating the spatial extent of influence for the neuron. The overall layout is symmetrical and hierarchical, with clear visual flow from input (Layer l) through intermediate (Layer l+1) to output (Layer l+2). The figure caption reinforces that the method employs small-size quasi-hexagonal kernels and highlights the key insight: the induced receptive field pattern remains unchanged regardless of the order in which the same kernel patterns are applied across layers.

The figure presents four distinct methodologies (labeled a, b, c, d) for training deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify 2D radiology images into different topic categories, using text from radiology reports as supervisory signals. Each panel illustrates a different level of text granularity and topic modeling approach.

In panel (a), the process begins with a set of documents (radiology reports), which undergo Natural Language Processing (NLP) to extract images mentioned within them (~216k images). These documents are then subjected to LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation) document topic clustering, resulting in a set of high-level topics (e.g., topic 0 with keywords 'protocol, abdomen', topic 2 with 'kidney, renal', etc.). Each topic is associated with its corresponding images. These image-topic pairs are used to train a deep CNN to classify 2D radiology images into these document-level topic categories. The CNN is depicted as a vertical, light green gradient rectangle labeled 'deep convolutional neural network'.

Panel (b) extends this approach by introducing hierarchical topic modeling. After initial LDA document topic clustering, each document topic is further subdivided into 10 sub-topics using LDA topic modeling on each document topic cluster (h2-LDA). For example, topic 0 splits into sub-topics 0-0 through 0-9, and similarly for other topics. These sub-topics are then associated with images, and the resulting image-subtopic pairs are used to train a deep CNN (shown as a vertical, light orange gradient rectangle) to classify images into finer-grained sub-topic categories.

Panel (c) focuses on sentence-level topic modeling. Documents are processed via NLP to extract sentences mentioning findings and their preceding/following sentences. These sentences are then clustered using LDA at the sentence level, producing a large number of sentence-level topics (e.g., topic 0 with 'radiographically', topic 1 with 'perinephric', up to topic 999 with 'seroma'). Images mentioned in these sentences (~187k images) are associated with their respective sentence-level topics. This association is used to train a deep CNN (vertical, light purple gradient rectangle) to classify images based on sentence-level topics.

Panel (d) introduces an image-to-word model. Radiology reports are processed via NLP to extract sentences mentioning findings. These sentences are linked to images mentioned within them. A disease ontology is used to identify two disease-related terms per sentence (e.g., 'which node'). A recurrent neural network maps words to vectors, creating a word2vec representation. The text-vector output layer of a pre-trained image-to-sentence-level-topic CNN is fine-tuned to output a vector closest to the target vector representing the disease in the image. This fine-tuned model is then used to perform topic clustering of images based on sentence-level LDA, and the resulting image-topic pairs are used to train another deep CNN (vertical, light purple gradient rectangle) to classify images into topic categories. All panels show a consistent flow: text processing → topic modeling → image association → CNN training, with arrows indicating data flow and training direction.

The figure presents a complete flow diagram of the Recursive Context Propagation Network (RCPN) for semantic segmentation, structured into two main stages: Visual Feature Extraction and Recursive Context Propagation Network (RCPN), separated by a dashed vertical boundary.

[1] Global Layout and Structure:
The diagram is horizontally organized from left to right, depicting the data flow through the network. The left section, labeled 'Visual Feature Extraction', processes an input image I to generate visual features V. The right section, labeled 'Recursive Context Propagation Network (RCPN)', performs iterative context propagation and refinement using these features. The final output is compared against ground truth for error computation.

[2] Visual Modules and Attributes:
In the Visual Feature Extraction stage, an input image I (a sailboat scene) passes through an orange rectangular module labeled F_CNN, representing a convolutional neural network. Its output is combined with a gray 3D block labeled V (visual feature map) via a summation operator (+). Below this, a colorful segmented image labeled 'superpixels' indicates region-based processing. From this stage, multiple visual feature streams v_1, v_2, ..., v_s are extracted and fed into the RCPN.

In the RCPN stage, each v_i enters a light blue rectangular module labeled F_sem (semantic feature extractor). Outputs x_1, x_2, ..., x_s from these modules feed into a recursive structure. Each x_i connects to a pink rectangular module labeled F_com (context combiner), which merges features across levels. For example, x_1 feeds into F_com to produce x_12; x_2 also feeds into F_com to produce x_3; and x_12 and x_3 feed into another F_com to produce x_123, illustrating recursive combination. These combined features then pass through light green rectangular modules labeled F_dec (decoder), generating reconstructed outputs x̃_1, x̃_12, x̃_3, ..., x̃_s. Each reconstructed output is processed by a purple rectangular module labeled F_lab (label classifier) to produce a predicted segmentation.

A red dashed arrow labeled 'Bypass error' runs from x̃_1 back to x_1, indicating a feedback mechanism for error propagation. On the far right, the predicted segmentations are compared with ground truth images (two versions shown: one with green hill, one with green sail) via a red circular subtraction operator (−), producing a 'Classifier Error' signal, highlighted in red text and arrows.

[3] Connections and Arrows:
Solid black arrows indicate forward propagation: from I → F_CNN → V → + → v_i → F_sem → x_i → F_com → x_ij → F_dec → x̃_ij → F_lab → Predicted. The recursive structure uses branching connections: x_1 and x_2 both feed into F_com to form x_12; x_12 and x_3 feed into another F_com to form x_123, etc. A red dashed arrow labeled 'Bypass error' loops from x̃_1 back to x_1, suggesting error feedback. Red solid arrows connect the predicted outputs and ground truth to the subtraction node, which outputs the 'Classifier Error'. This error signal is visually emphasized with bold red lines and text, indicating its role in training or refinement.

The figure presents an overview of the Horde architecture, a framework for learning an ensemble of reward shapings in reinforcement learning. The global layout is structured as a flowchart with distinct modules arranged from top-left to bottom-right, depicting a data and control flow from the environment through shaping, scaling, function approximation, and finally to an ensemble policy. The top-left corner contains a green oval labeled 'Behavior' enclosing an 'Environment' ellipse, indicating the interaction loop between state s, action a, and next state s'. This environment outputs the raw reward R and the transition tuple (s, a, s') to downstream components.

The main processing pipeline begins with the 'Shaping' module, which receives the raw reward R and the current state s. A designer input, denoted by the symbol Φ, is fed into Shaping, which then produces multiple shaping functions Φ₁, ..., Φᵢ, ..., Φₗ. These are passed to the 'Scaling' module, which also receives a control signal C. The Scaling module applies scalar coefficients c¹₁, ..., cᵢⱼ, ..., cₗₖₗ to each shaping function, producing scaled rewards R, R¹₁, ..., Rᵢⱼ, ..., Rₗₖₗ. These scaled rewards are represented as bold lines, indicating they are vectors.

Below the Shaping and Scaling modules lies the 'Function Approximation' block, which takes the transition (s, a, s') as input. It outputs a set of blue horizontal lines representing feature vectors derived from the transition. These features are connected via vertical green lines labeled θ₀, θ¹₁, ..., θᵢⱼ, ..., θₗₖₗ, which represent weight parameters for individual learners. Each intersection of a green line (weight) with a blue line (feature) corresponds to a weighted feature for a specific learner.

Each learner is represented by an inverted blue triangle labeled d₀, d¹₁, ..., dᵢⱼ, ..., dₗₖₗ. Each triangle receives its corresponding scaled reward (R, R¹₁, etc.) and computes a policy π₀, π¹₁, ..., πᵢⱼ, ..., πₗₖₗ, shown as red downward arrows. These policies are then aggregated into an 'Ensemble' module, depicted as a rounded rectangle, which combines them to produce the final 'Ensemble policy'.

A feedback loop is shown: the output of the Ensemble, labeled a', is a vector of greedy actions at state s' with respect to each policy πᵢⱼ. This vector feeds back into the Environment, closing the learning loop. The caption clarifies that in this latent setting, all environmental interactions occur only in the upper-left corner, meaning the rest of the architecture operates on learned representations. The diagram uses color coding—green for weights, blue for features, red for policies, and bold black lines for reward vectors—to distinguish different types of signals.

The figure illustrates a deep learning framework for fine-grained classification using triplet-based training with shared parameters across three convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The global layout is left-to-right, starting with the input data on the far left, progressing through three parallel CNN branches, followed by normalization, structured label embedding, and finally loss computation on the right. The entire pipeline is designed to learn discriminative features and a fine-grained classifier by jointly optimizing two loss functions.

On the left, the 'Training Data' is represented as a vertical stack of horizontal bars, each colored blue, green, or red, corresponding to reference (ref), positive (pos), and negative (neg) images respectively, as indicated by the legend above. These triplets are fed into three parallel CNNs labeled R (blue), P (green), and N (red), which share the same network architecture and parameters, as denoted by the label 'Parameters Sharing CNN'. Each CNN consists of multiple fully connected layers depicted as interconnected nodes, with the final layer being a dense, fully connected layer.

The outputs from each of the three CNNs are passed through individual L2 normalization blocks, shown as gray rectangular boxes labeled 'ℓ₂', to normalize the feature vectors. These normalized features are then combined and fed into a module labeled 'Structured Label', enclosed in a purple rounded rectangle. This module visualizes the hierarchical or attribute-based structure of the labels: at the top, a row of three circles (blue, green, red) represents the triplet classes; below, two groups of three circles each (with overlapping colors) indicate shared or hierarchical relationships; further down, four geometric shapes (hexagon, star, square, star) are connected to the lower label groups, symbolizing higher-level semantic or structural attributes.

From the 'Structured Label' module, two loss components are computed. The first is 'Softmax with Loss', shown in an orange box, which computes the standard classification loss. The second is 'Generalized Triplet Loss', also in an orange box, which enforces discriminative feature learning based on the triplet structure. A plus sign between these two boxes indicates that they are summed together for joint optimization. The final block, labeled 'Loss Computation', signifies the overall objective function that combines both losses to train the model. The entire process is designed to simultaneously learn robust feature representations and a fine-grained classifier by leveraging both class labels and their underlying structural relationships.

The figure illustrates the initial synaptic weight configuration for a neural network controlling a robot's movement behavior, specifically designed to enforce an attraction response. The global layout is a two-layer feedforward network with four input neurons at the top and two output motor neurons at the bottom. The top layer consists of two pairs of sensor neurons: 'Left Food Sensor Neurons' and 'Right Food Sensor Neurons' on the left side, and 'Left Container Neurons' and 'Right Container Neurons' on the right side. These are represented as light green rectangular boxes with black borders and black text. The bottom layer contains two motor neurons: 'Left Motor Neurons' and 'Right Motor Neurons', also depicted as light green rectangles with black borders and black text. All connections between the top and bottom layers are shown as arrows indicating directed influence. Solid black arrows represent synapses set to maximum strength, while dashed blue arrows indicate synapses set to zero. Specifically, each food sensor neuron connects with a solid arrow to the motor neuron on the same side (e.g., Left Food Sensor Neurons → Left Motor Neurons), and each container neuron connects with a solid arrow to the opposite-side motor neuron (e.g., Left Container Neurons → Right Motor Neurons). Additionally, cross-connections from food sensors to the opposite motor neuron and from container neurons to the same-side motor neuron are shown as dashed blue lines, signifying they are disabled (set to zero). A legend box on the far right, outlined in black, clarifies the meaning of the arrow types: a solid black downward arrow labeled 'Synapses Set to Maximum' and a dashed blue downward arrow labeled 'Synapses Set to Zero'. This setup ensures that food detection activates the corresponding side’s motor, promoting movement toward food, while container detection activates the opposite motor, causing the robot to turn away from containers. The overall structure is symmetrical and clearly organized to reflect the intended behavioral logic: attraction to food and avoidance of containers.

The figure presents an end-to-end neural network architecture for image captioning, structured into two main horizontal pathways: a top-level processing flow and a detailed Localization Layer at the bottom. The global layout begins on the left with an input image of dimensions 3×W×H, depicted as a photograph of two cats watching a TV screen. This image feeds into a gray trapezoidal block labeled 'CNN', which outputs convolutional features represented as a light blue cube with dimensions C×W'×H'.

From the CNN output, the top pathway proceeds through a vertical purple rectangular block, symbolizing further feature processing, leading to region features shown as stacked green and blue cubes with dimensions B×C×X×Y. These are then passed through a 'Recognition Network' (represented by three vertical black bars), which produces region codes of size B×D. These region codes are fed into an LSTM (gray rectangle), which generates descriptive captions such as 'Striped gray cat' (green box) and 'Cats watching TV' (blue box), displayed alongside a cropped image with bounding boxes.

The bottom half of the diagram details the 'Localization Layer', enclosed in a large lavender rounded rectangle. It takes the same CNN output (light blue cube, C×W'×H') as input. Inside this layer, a gray trapezoid labeled 'Conv' processes the features to produce 'Region Proposals' (4k×W'×H'), visualized as a grid with a star indicating a selected region. Concurrently, 'Region scores' (k×W'×H') are generated from the Conv output. These scores guide the selection of 'Best Proposals' (B×4), shown as two overlapping rectangles (one green, one blue), via a 'Sampling' step.

The Best Proposals are then fed into a 'Grid Generator', which creates a 'Sampling Grid' (B×X×Y×2), illustrated as a grid of dots. This grid, along with the original conv features, is input into a 'Bilinear Sampler' (a gray circle with an 'X' inside), which extracts the final 'Region features' (B×512×7×7), shown as stacked green and blue cubes. These features match those in the top pathway and feed into the Recognition Network.

Connections are indicated by solid black arrows showing data flow: from image to CNN, through the Localization Layer components, and up to the LSTM. A dashed line connects the top pathway's Recognition Network to the Localization Layer, emphasizing its role in generating region features. The LSTM has a feedback loop arrow pointing back to itself, indicating recurrent processing. All blocks are labeled with their function or data dimension, and the entire model is trained end-to-end with gradient descent.

The figure presents an overview of a joint image-text topic detection and tracking framework for news content. The global layout is structured as a top-down pipeline divided into three main stages: preprocessing, topic detection, and topic tracking, separated by dashed horizontal lines. At the top, two input sources are shown: 'News Videos', represented by a collage of video frames depicting news anchors and scenes, and 'News Captions', shown as a block of sample text from news broadcasts. Both inputs flow downward via blue arrows into a rectangular box labeled 'Preprocessing: Segmentation', indicating initial processing steps such as splitting videos and texts into manageable segments.

Following preprocessing, the pipeline enters the 'Topic Detection' stage, enclosed in a large rounded rectangle. This stage is titled 'Joint Image-Text Topic Detection with And-Or Graph Representation by Swendsen-Wang Cuts Cluster Sampling'. It illustrates the detection of topics across multiple time periods, labeled 'Topics Detected in Time Period 1' and 'Topics Detected in Time Period M', with ellipses suggesting intermediate periods. Each time period contains one or more topics (e.g., 'Topic 1-1', 'Topic M-1'), each represented as an And-Or graph. These graphs have circular nodes: the root node splits into 'Text' and 'Image' branches. The 'Text' branch further divides into 'Who', 'Where', and 'What' sub-nodes, while the 'Image' branch splits into 'Face' and 'Object'. Each of these leaf nodes connects to small square boxes representing specific entities or features. Red dashed lines connect related entities across the text and image branches, indicating joint semantic associations. The entire structure under this stage is labeled 'Detected Topics'.

The output of topic detection feeds into the next stage, 'Topic Tracking', also enclosed in a rounded rectangle. This stage is labeled 'Joint Image-Text Topic Tracking'. It visualizes the temporal evolution of topics using a sequence of circular nodes arranged horizontally. Multiple colored paths (blue, orange, green, purple) connect these nodes, illustrating how individual topics evolve, merge, split, or disappear over time. These paths represent 'Topic Trajectories', as labeled at the bottom right. The figure uses consistent visual attributes: blue arrows denote data flow; circular nodes represent topics or topic components; square nodes represent atomic features; and dashed red lines indicate cross-modal associations. The overall design emphasizes the integration of visual and textual modalities for coherent topic modeling and longitudinal tracking.

The figure illustrates an end-to-end deep neural network architecture designed for generating natural language descriptions from video sequences. The global layout is horizontal and sequential, depicting a pipeline that processes multiple video frames over time, each frame being analyzed at multiple spatial scales before being fed into a recurrent network for sentence generation. On the left side, three parallel processing streams labeled 'scale 1', 'scale 2', and 'scale 3' represent different spatial resolutions of the same video frame, shown as progressively larger images of a cat and a bear interacting in a wooded environment. Each scale feeds into a shared convolutional backbone labeled 'conv 1–5', represented as a beige trapezoid, indicating feature extraction from the raw pixel data.

From each scale, the features are passed through a series of fully connected or convolutional layers. For scale 1, the outputs are labeled 'fc6', 'fc7', and 'fc8', depicted as small beige cubes with dimensions '1×K', '1×K', and '1×N' respectively. For scales 2 and 3, the layers are labeled 'conv-fc6', 'conv-fc7', and 'conv-fc8', shown as larger beige cubes with dimensions '8×8×K', '8×8×K', '8×8×N' for scale 2, and '16×16×K', '16×16×K', '16×16×N' for scale 3. These dimensions reflect the spatial extent of the feature maps at each scale. The outputs from each scale’s final layer are then pooled using a max-pooling operation, represented by a light orange hexagon labeled 'max', reducing each to a '1×N' vector. These pooled vectors from all scales are combined via another max-pooling operation to produce a single '1×N' semantic vector per frame.

This process is repeated for consecutive frames, labeled 'frame t−1', 'frame t', and 'frame t+1', with each frame's '1×N' vector feeding into a central green rounded rectangle labeled 'Recurrent Network'. This module integrates temporal information across frames and generates a sequence of words as output, shown on the far right as 'A cat and a bear meet in the woods'. The recurrent network is depicted as a single block, implying it maintains internal state across time steps to produce coherent sentences.

The visual modules use consistent shapes and colors: trapezoids for convolutional backbones, cubes for feature representations (beige for shared AlexNet parameters, white for learned layers), hexagons for pooling operations, and a rounded rectangle for the recurrent decoder. Text labels are placed directly below or beside each module, with dimensions annotated above or beside the cubes. Arrows indicate the flow of data from left to right, with branching paths for multi-scale processing and merging paths for pooling. The diagram emphasizes the multi-scale, multi-instance nature of the feature extraction, contrasting with the top stream (single-scale) which uses only fc layers and does not include spatial pooling. The caption clarifies that this architecture handles ambiguity in object count, size, and location, leveraging shared parameters from AlexNet (shaded components) and producing high-level semantic embeddings for each frame before decoding into natural language.

The figure presents two architectural diagrams, labeled (a) tagCNN and (b) inCNN, illustrating variations of a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based encoder for a joint language model (LM) task, likely for named entity recognition or relation extraction. Both diagrams share a common top-level structure: a deep neural network (DNN) that takes input features and outputs a prediction, here shown as the word 'presidential' from a green box at the top. The DNN is represented as a light blue rectangular region containing four white boxes connected in a horizontal row, which feed into a single output node.

In diagram (a) tagCNN, the input consists of a sequence of six tokens: '智利', '举行', '国会', '与', '总统', '选举', each represented by a gray box labeled z₁ through z₆. These tokens are processed by a module labeled 'convolution & gating' within a light green background area marked 'tagCNN'. This module produces four feature vectors, e₂, e₃, e₄, and an unlabeled gray box, which are then fed into the DNN. The text 'holds parliament and' is placed below these feature vectors, indicating their semantic content. The arrows show a unidirectional flow from the token sequence up through the convolution & gating layer to the DNN.

Diagram (b) inCNN introduces a modification. It retains the same token sequence and convolution & gating module, but adds a new component: a dark blue box labeled h({e₂,e₃,e₄}) positioned before the token sequence. This box represents a contextualized representation derived from the features e₂, e₃, and e₄, which are now enclosed in a dashed rectangle to indicate they are the source of this context. A horizontal arrow connects this blue box to the first token z₁, suggesting that the contextual information is injected into the input sequence. The rest of the architecture remains identical to tagCNN, with the same DNN and output. The label 'inCNN' is placed in a light gray background area, distinguishing it from tagCNN. The overall layout is side-by-side comparison, with both diagrams sharing the same vertical flow from bottom to top, emphasizing the difference in how context is incorporated into the input sequence.

The figure illustrates a hybrid preference prediction scheme that integrates visual content analysis with collaborative filtering, enabling predictions even when no past user ratings are available. The global layout is horizontal, progressing from left to right through five main stages: Query, Visual space, Latent space (Q), Collaborative filtering, and Prediction/Raters. Two parallel pathways are shown: one for queries with visual input only (top path), and another for queries with past ratings (bottom path), which converge into a unified latent space and prediction mechanism.

In the 'Query' section on the far left, two input types are presented: a visual query (a face image with a blue bounding box) and an alternative input of past ratings (represented by green thumbs-up and red thumbs-down icons). These inputs feed into distinct initial processing steps. The visual query enters the 'Visual space', depicted as a grid of thumbnail images, where a 'Nearest neighbor' search identifies visually similar images (highlighted with a green border around the target). This visual similarity is then mapped via 'Regression' into the 'Latent space (Q)', represented as a scatter plot of black dots with one highlighted point (gold) corresponding to the query’s latent representation. The bottom pathway, starting from 'Past ratings', uses 'Matrix factorization' (indicated by a thick blue curved arrow) to directly map the rating history into the same latent space, shown as a blue dot within the scatter plot.

The latent space (Q) serves as the central hub where both pathways converge. From here, a collaborative filtering step is applied. This is visualized as a matrix multiplication operation: a matrix labeled p^T (containing user-item interaction scores) is multiplied by a vector Q (representing the query’s latent embedding), yielding a prediction vector. The matrix p^T is shown as a 5x8 grid of decimal values (e.g., 4.0, 8.4, 2.5...), while Q is a vertical vector of seven decimal values (e.g., 8.2, 1.8, 7.0...). The result is a vertical vector of predicted scores (e.g., 6.7, 3.9, 7.4...), which are then mapped to binary predictions (thumbs-up or thumbs-down) in the 'Prediction' column. The final 'Raters' column displays four user faces, each aligned with a prediction, indicating whether the model predicts they would like (green thumb) or dislike (red thumb) the query item.

Connections between modules are indicated by arrows: brown arrows represent the visual-to-latent regression path, while thick blue arrows denote the matrix factorization path from past ratings to latent space. The collaborative filtering step is shown with a large black multiplication symbol (×) between the matrices. The figure caption clarifies that this scheme allows visual queries without prior ratings to be regressed into the latent space—derived from matrix factorization of known ratings—and then processed identically to queries with known ratings, enabling consistent preference predictions.

The figure illustrates the architecture of a system combining Redis with KVolve, designed to manage key-value operations with versioning and update specifications. The global layout is divided into two main regions: on the left, three client entities (ClientX, ClientU, ClientY) are shown initiating operations; on the right, a large cylindrical data store labeled 'Redis + KVolve' represents the backend storage system. The clients are arranged vertically, each performing a distinct operation: ClientX attempts a 'get k:x', ClientU performs an 'upd k: v0 → v1', and ClientY executes a 'get k:y'. Each client box is outlined in blue, with the operation text inside, and a gray italicized label below indicating the client's current view of the key-value state (e.g., ClientX {k:v0}).

Within the Redis + KVolve cylinder, the internal structure shows key-value pairs stored as gray rectangular boxes. For key 'k:x', there is a value 'valX v0' connected by a dashed blue arrow from the key, indicating the current value. Similarly, for key 'k:y', two values are shown: 'valY v0' (grayed out with a red 'X' over the connecting arrow) and 'valYupd v1' (active, connected by a solid dashed blue arrow), representing a versioned update. A light blue rectangular box labeled 'upd spec: {val' = val + "upd"}' is positioned within the cylinder, signifying the update specification logic applied during updates.

Connections between components are represented by black arrows with labels indicating the action type. From ClientX, a black arrow labeled 'close' points to the 'upd spec' box, and another arrow from ClientX to the 'k:x' key is crossed out with a red circle, indicating a failed or blocked get operation. From ClientU, a black arrow labeled 'install' points to the 'upd spec' box, showing the installation of the update rule. From ClientY, a black arrow points to the 'k:y' key, which then connects via a dashed blue arrow to 'valYupd v1', indicating a successful retrieval of the updated value. The red 'X' over the dashed arrow from 'k:y' to 'valY v0' visually denotes that the old version is no longer accessible or has been invalidated. The visual attributes include color coding: blue outlines for clients, light blue for update specification, gray for stored values, and red for failure indicators. The diagram effectively conveys a versioned key-value system where updates are specified and installed, and clients may observe different versions based on their access timing and update installation status.

The figure illustrates a two-stage deep learning framework for saliency detection, structured into two main phases: coarse representation learning and fine representation learning. The global layout is left-to-right, beginning with an input image on the far left and progressing through two sequential processing stages enclosed in dashed boundary boxes—blue for coarse learning and green for fine learning—before producing the final saliency map on the far right.

On the left, the input is a color photograph of two people against a cityscape background. Below it, a superpixel segmentation result is shown, depicted as a red-and-black overlay highlighting segmented regions. An arrow from the original image points to the coarse representation learning stage, which is enclosed in a blue dashed oval. The figure illustrates a dual-classifier framework for learning visually grounded predictions from noisy human-centric annotations. The global layout is left-to-right, beginning with an input image of bananas labeled with concepts 'Banana' and 'Yellow'. This image feeds into a ConvNet, whose fc7 layer outputs feature representations used by two parallel classifiers: the Visual Presence Classifier v^w and the Relevance Classifier r^w. Both classifiers operate for each concept w ∈ {Banana, Yellow}. 

The Visual Presence Classifier consists of a Linear layer followed by a Sigmoid activation, producing v^w(z^w|I), which estimates the probability that concept w is visually present in image I. Its output is visualized as a bar chart under 'Visually Grounded Predictions v(z|I)', showing green (Banana) and yellow (Yellow) bars indicating confidence scores.

The Relevance Classifier processes the same fc7 features through a Linear layer, then Softmax to compute s_ij, followed by 'Division by Marginal' to produce r^w(y^w,z^w|I), modeling the conditional probability that a human would mention concept w given its visual presence or absence. This leads to a bar chart labeled 'Conditional estimates r_ij', showing two scenarios: z^w=0 (concept not visually present) and z^w=1 (visually present), with corresponding green and yellow bars indicating relevance probabilities.

These two outputs are combined via a 'Marginalize' operation, which integrates over possible visual states to produce the final 'Human-Centric Predictions h(y|I)', represented as another bar chart with green and yellow bars. This output is compared against available human-centric ground truth y to compute loss, enabling backpropagation for training.

On the left, a table contrasts visually correct ground truth z (both concepts present, marked with green checkmarks) with available human-centric ground truth y (only 'Banana' marked, 'Yellow' marked with red X), emphasizing the noisy nature of the human labels. The model outputs v and h correspond to the visual presence and human-centric predictions respectively. Dashed lines indicate backpropagation paths for training. The entire pipeline is designed to learn robust visual classifiers despite lacking direct access to visually accurate labels.

The figure illustrates a multi-stream deep learning framework for video classification, structured into three parallel processing streams: spatial, motion, and audio. The global layout is vertically stacked, with each stream occupying a distinct horizontal section, all converging toward a final prediction module on the right. Each stream begins with an input modality—individual frames for the spatial stream, stacked optical flow for the motion stream, and audio spectrogram for the audio stream—followed by a convolutional neural network (ConvNet), then a recurrent neural network (LSTM) layer, and finally feeding into a shared prediction block.

In the top stream, labeled 'Spatial', an individual frame (depicted as a small image of a person in action) is processed by a Spatial ConvNet, represented by a sequence of 3D blocks in blue, orange, and pink, symbolizing convolutional layers. The output features are passed through a two-layer LSTM network, shown as a grid of light green hexagonal nodes arranged in two rows, with arrows indicating sequential processing from left to right and top to bottom. A red dashed box highlights the final feature vector from the last LSTM unit.

The middle stream, labeled 'Motion', takes stacked optical flow (shown as multiple red-tinted frames with motion blur) as input. This is processed by a Motion ConvNet, visually identical in structure to the Spatial ConvNet but labeled differently. Its output feeds into a similar two-layer LSTM network, also composed of light green hexagonal nodes, with the same red dashed box marking the final feature vector.

The bottom stream, labeled 'Audio', processes an audio spectrogram (displayed as a colorful heatmap with frequency over time) through an Audio ConvNet, again using the same 3D block representation. The output features are not passed through an LSTM in this stream, as indicated by the absence of the LSTM grid; instead, the final feature vector from the ConvNet is directly forwarded.

All three streams converge at a central module labeled 'Prediction with Adaptive Fusion', depicted as a white rectangular box with a curved bottom edge. Solid black arrows connect the red-dashed-boxed outputs from each stream to this fusion module, indicating that the final prediction is made by adaptively combining the features from all three modalities. The overall design emphasizes parallel processing of different sensory inputs followed by late fusion for enhanced classification performance.

The figure illustrates the architecture of a Scale-Aware Feature R-CNN (SAF R-CNN), designed for object detection with improved performance across different object scales. The global layout is left-to-right, starting with an input image on the far left, progressing through a shared backbone network, and then branching into two parallel sub-networks — a large-size and a small-size sub-network — before converging at the final output stage. The input image, shown as a 3D tensor with dimensions 3 (channels) and spatial dimensions implied by the context, is processed by a series of convolutional and max-pooling layers, represented as 3D blocks with decreasing spatial dimensions (64, 128, 256) and consistent channel depth (3). These layers extract general features from the entire image, with dashed lines indicating intermediate layers not fully drawn. A cropped region from the input, highlighted with a green bounding box, is shown as a sample object proposal, which is then passed to a 'Scale-aware Weighting' module. This module takes the height of the proposal as input and outputs two weights, labeled 'Weight1' (in blue) and 'Weight2' (in green), which are used later to combine the outputs of the two sub-networks.

The architecture then splits into two parallel branches enclosed in dashed boxes: the 'Large-size Sub-network' (blue outline) and the 'Small-size Sub-network' (green outline). Both sub-networks receive the same feature maps from the shared backbone but process them independently. Each branch begins with two 3D convolutional layers (each with 512 channels), followed by an RoI pooling layer that converts variable-sized region proposals into fixed-length feature vectors (4096-dimensional). These are then fed into two fully connected layers (also 4096-dimensional), after which the network branches into two output layers: one for classification scores (labeled 'cls_score' or 'S_cls_score'/'L_cls_score') and another for bounding box predictions ('bbox_pred' or 'S_bbox_pred'/'L_bbox_pred'). The classification output has dimension 2 (implying binary classification or K+1 classes including background), while the bounding box output has dimension 8 (likely representing 4 coordinates per class for K=2 classes). The outputs from both sub-networks are combined using the weights generated by the scale-aware weighting module: the large-size branch's outputs are multiplied by 'Weight1' (blue arrows), and the small-size branch's outputs are multiplied by 'Weight2' (green arrows). The weighted outputs are summed to produce the final classification score probabilities ('cls_prob') and final bounding box predictions ('bbox_pred'), which are the final detection results. The visual modules use distinct colors (blue for large-size, green for small-size) to differentiate the two paths, and all connections are directed with solid arrows, indicating the flow of data. The figure includes numerical labels for feature dimensions and layer names, ensuring clarity in the model structure.

The figure illustrates the unrolled architecture of a CST-VAE (Conditional Style Transfer Variational Autoencoder) network for processing multiple image layers, specifically shown for two layers (L₁ and L₂). The global layout is horizontal and sequential, with each layer processed independently but sharing a common structure. Each layer’s processing pipeline is vertically stacked and mirrored across layers, with connections feeding into a final LayerComposite module at the bottom.

Each layer begins with an input Δᵢ (where i=1,2), represented as a gray circle for Δ₁=x and a white circle for Δ₂, indicating the initial input or condition for that layer. From this input, two parallel branches diverge: one for pose encoding and one for content encoding. These branches are visually grouped using dashed rectangular boxes with distinct colors: green for Pose Encoder and red for Content Encoder, as indicated in the legend on the right.

In the Pose Encoder branch (green), the input Δᵢ is fed into a Spatial Transformer Network (STN) block labeled STN(Δᵢ,T̂ᵢ), which outputs an estimated pose representation T̂ᵢ. This is followed by a Gaussian distribution module μₜᵢ, σ²ₜᵢ, from which a latent variable zᵀᵢ is sampled. This sample is then decoded through a Pose Decoder (blue dashed box) to produce the final pose output Tᵢ.

Similarly, in the Content Encoder branch (red), the same input Δᵢ is processed through another STN block, STN(Δᵢ,T̂ᵢ), producing an estimated content representation Ĉᵢ. This feeds into a Gaussian distribution module μ꜀ᵢ, σ²꜀ᵢ, from which a latent variable z꜀ᵢ is sampled. This sample is decoded via a Content Decoder (purple dashed box) to yield the final content output Cᵢ.

After decoding, both Tᵢ and Cᵢ are fed into another STN block, labeled STN(Cᵢ,Tᵢ), which spatially aligns the content based on the pose. The output of this alignment is passed to a loss node Lᵢ (a circular node), which computes the reconstruction or alignment loss for that layer.

The losses L₁ and L₂ are connected via thick black curves to the next layer’s input (Δ₂), suggesting a feedback or conditional mechanism where the output of one layer influences the next. Finally, all layer outputs (L₁, L₂, etc.) are combined into a single LayerComposite module at the bottom, represented as a gray dashed rectangle, which likely performs final composition or aggregation of the processed layers.

The figure uses consistent visual attributes: circles for nodes, dashed rectangles for encoder/decoder modules, and labeled arrows for data flow. The legend on the right clarifies the color coding: green for Pose Encoder, red for Content Encoder, blue for Pose Decoder, and purple for Content Decoder. The entire diagram is designed to show how the CST-VAE processes image layers sequentially while maintaining pose-content disentanglement and spatial alignment.

The figure illustrates the architecture of an HT (Hierarchical Transformation) model, which is a convolutional arithmetic circuit designed to implement hierarchical decomposition. The global layout is a left-to-right sequential pipeline, starting from an input X and progressing through multiple hidden layers to a final dense output layer. The structure is modular, with each stage clearly labeled and connected by directed arrows indicating data flow.

The process begins with the 'input X', represented as a light blue cube containing a green inner cube labeled x_i. This input is transformed into a 'representation' module, also a light blue cube, where a red inner cube represents the learned representation. A green arrow connects the input to the representation, and below it, the equation rep(i,d) = f_{θ_d}(x_i) defines the representation function, where θ_d denotes learnable parameters.

Following the representation, the architecture enters a series of hidden layers, starting with 'hidden layer 0' and ending with 'hidden layer L-1', where L = log₂N. Each hidden layer consists of two main components: a '1x1 conv' block and a 'pooling' block, both depicted as light blue cubes. In hidden layer 0, the 1x1 conv block contains a red dot and a yellow square, while the pooling block contains a yellow dot. The 1x1 conv operation is defined by the equation conv₀(j,γ) = ⟨a^{0,j,γ}, rep(j,:)⟩, representing an inner product between a weight vector a and the representation. The pooling operation is defined as pool₀(j,γ) = ∏_{j'∈{2j−1,2j}} conv₀(j',γ), indicating a product over two adjacent conv outputs.

This pattern repeats across subsequent hidden layers, indicated by ellipsis (...), until the final hidden layer, labeled 'hidden layer L-1'. Here, the 1x1 conv block contains a yellow square, and the pooling block contains a red cube with a yellow dot inside. The pooling operation at this layer is given by pool_{L−1}(γ) = ∏_{j'∈{1,2}} conv_{L−1}(j',γ), showing a product over two inputs.

Finally, the output from the last pooling block is fed into a 'dense (output)' layer, represented as a light blue cube with a red dot inside, labeled Y. The output is computed as out(y) = ⟨a^{L,y}, pool_{L−1}(:)⟩, an inner product between a weight vector a and the pooled feature vector.

All connections are shown as arrows: green for the initial transformation, brown for conv-to-pool within each layer, and red for the final connection to the output. The modules are consistently styled with light blue outer cubes and colored inner elements (green, red, yellow) to denote different data or operations. Text labels are placed above or beside each module, and mathematical equations are positioned below corresponding blocks to define the operations precisely.

The figure illustrates a hybrid neural network architecture combining a scene feature extraction module with a modified Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) unit, referred to as SF-LSTM (Scene-Factorized LSTM). The global layout is divided into two main parts: on the left, a scene vector extraction pipeline; on the right, the SF-LSTM cell structure enclosed within a dashed red rectangle.

On the left side, an input image depicting a baseball scene is processed by a 'Places-205 CNN' model, represented as a light green rounded rectangle. The output of this CNN is fed into a '2-layer MLP' (also a light green rounded rectangle), which generates a scene vector denoted as 's', shown as a white circle. This scene vector 's' is then used to modulate the internal operations of the SF-LSTM cell.

The right side of the diagram details the SF-LSTM cell. It receives inputs from two sources: the previous hidden state h_{t-1} and the current input x_t, both presented as stacked boxes. These inputs are combined and fed into three gates: the input gate 'i', the forget gate 'f', and the output gate 'o', each represented as a light green circle. Additionally, a tanh activation function is applied to the concatenated input (h_{t-1}, x_t), producing a candidate cell state, which is then multiplied by the input gate 'i' via a gold-colored multiplication node (marked with an 'X').

The forget gate 'f' multiplies the previous cell state c_{t-1} (represented as a light green circle) through another gold multiplication node, and the result is added to the input gate's output to produce the new cell state c_t. The new cell state c_t is then passed through the output gate 'o' via a third gold multiplication node, and the result is activated by a tanh function (implied) to produce the new hidden state h_t, shown as a white box.

Crucially, the scene vector 's' is connected via dashed blue lines to all three gates (i, f, o), indicating that it modulates or factorizes the weight matrices of these gates, as described in the caption. This factorization allows the scene context to influence the gating decisions dynamically. The internal flow of the cell state c_t is shown with a curved black arrow looping back from c_t to c_{t-1}, representing the memory retention mechanism. All connections between components are indicated by solid black arrows, except for the modulatory connections from 's' to the gates, which are dashed blue lines. The entire SF-LSTM cell is labeled with bold text 'SF-LSTM' at the top center of the dashed red boundary.

The figure illustrates the overall procedure of a discriminative and generative tracking algorithm that leverages a pre-trained CNN for feature extraction and target localization. The entire process is iterative, with the SVM and generative model being updated based on the current frame’s tracking result for subsequent frames. The connections are indicated by thick red arrows for forward and backward passes, gray arrows for weight propagation, and a red 'x' symbol for the interaction between the generative model and the target posterior. The figure illustrates the architecture of a multimodal caption generation model, composed of three main components: a Lexical Classifier, a Caption Model (which includes a Multimodal Unit), and a Language Model. This is followed by a Classification Layer (yellow rectangle), producing a feature vector denoted as f_I (white square). The CNN and classification layer are pre-trained using unpaired image data, as indicated by the legend.

The central Caption Model receives both the image feature f_I from the Lexical Classifier and a sequence of words from the Language Model. The figure illustrates a single Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) memory cell as proposed by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997). The entire structure is enclosed within a light blue rectangular box, representing the cell's boundary. Inside, there are five main circular nodes arranged vertically and horizontally, connected by various types of arrows indicating data flow and temporal dependencies.

At the bottom, a cyan circle labeled σ (sigmoid activation) receives input from outside the cell via dashed lines, representing the current input and previous time step’s output. This node outputs g_c^(t), which flows upward to a white circular node labeled Π (product operation). From this Π node, a solid blue arrow points to a cyan circle with a diagonal line through it, representing the internal state s_c^(t). This diagonal line signifies that the node applies the identity (linear) function. The equation s_c^(t) = g_c^(t) · i_c^(t) + s_c^(t−1) is written next to this node, indicating the update rule for the internal state, where i_c^(t) is the input gate and s_c^(t−1) is the previous state.

A blue dashed curved arrow loops back from the internal state node to itself, symbolizing the recurrent connection with a fixed unit weight, as explained in the legend. Above the internal state node, another white Π node receives two inputs: one from the internal state node and another from a second cyan σ node on the right, which outputs o_c^(t). This second σ node also receives external input via dashed lines, similar to the first σ node. The top Π node computes the product of its two inputs, and the resulting output v_c^(t) = s_c^(t) · o_c^(t) is shown at the top of the cell, with a magenta arrow pointing upward, indicating the cell’s output.

On the right side of the diagram, a legend clarifies the meaning of the different arrow styles: a black dashed arrow represents an edge to the next time step; a black dotted arrow represents an edge from the previous time step (and current input); and a solid blue arrow indicates a weight fixed at 1. All edges connecting to or from the Π nodes are solid blue, confirming their fixed unit weights. The overall layout follows a vertical flow from bottom to top, with horizontal connections for gating operations, and a recurrent loop for state persistence.

The figure illustrates the graphical structure of GMM-LDA, a generative model combining an intent model and a topic model to jointly model user intent and document topics. The overall layout is a hierarchical probabilistic graphical model, structured with nested plate notations indicating repeated elements over documents, document segments, and topics. The diagram is divided into two main components: the Intent Model on the left, enclosed in a dashed gray box, and the Topic Model on the right, also within a dashed gray box. These are connected through shared latent variables influencing the observed word variable w.

In the Intent Model, red-colored circular nodes represent latent variables and parameters. The hyperparameters λ and ρ feed into the latent variables u and v, respectively. From v, a dashed red arrow leads to π, which then influences z via a dashed red arrow. The variable u also connects to z with a dashed red arrow. The parameter α, enclosed in a red-bordered rectangle labeled K, represents a Dirichlet prior over K intent categories and has a solid red arrow pointing to z. The node z, a red circle, represents the latent intent variable for a segment.

In the Topic Model, blue-colored circular nodes denote latent variables and parameters. The parameter θ, a blue circle, represents the topic distribution for a document and is associated with a plate labeled D, indicating it is repeated for each document. From θ, a solid blue arrow points to t, the latent topic variable for a segment, which is inside a plate labeled N_d, signifying it is repeated for each segment within a document. The parameter β, enclosed in a blue-bordered rectangle labeled T, represents a Dirichlet prior over T topics and has a solid blue arrow pointing to t. The node t then connects to the observed word w via a solid blue arrow.

The central node w, shaded gray, represents the observed word and is influenced by multiple sources. It receives a solid red arrow from z (intent), a solid blue arrow from t (topic), and a solid black arrow from b, which in turn is influenced by γ, a top-level hyperparameter. The node b acts as a bias or global effect on word generation. The plate labeled N_ds indicates that the generation of w occurs for each word within a document segment, and this plate is nested within the N_d plate, which is itself nested within the D plate, reflecting the hierarchical structure of documents composed of segments composed of words.

Connections between the two models are established through the shared influence on w, with the intent model contributing via z and the topic model via t. The dashed arrows from u and π to z suggest conditional dependencies or soft influences, while solid arrows indicate direct generative relationships. The entire structure is designed to model how both user intent and document topic jointly determine the generation of words in a corpus.

The figure illustrates the architecture of a TDR (Time-Discrete Reservoir) with a multitask readout, structured into three main components labeled A, B, and C, arranged vertically from top to bottom. 

[1] Global Layout and Structure: The diagram is organized in a sequential, time-unrolled fashion across T time steps, indicated by the horizontal progression from left to right. Each time step t ∈ {1, ..., T} contains identical vertical stacks of modules A, B, and C. The entire structure is grouped into three distinct layers: A at the top, B in the middle, and C at the bottom. The time steps are visually separated by ellipses (...) between them, indicating repetition. On the far right, large curly braces group the corresponding modules across all time steps and label them A, B, and C respectively.

[2] Visual Modules and Attributes: 
- Module A (Input Layer): At the top, for each time step t, an external input z_t (represented as a black downward arrow) feeds into a light green rectangular box labeled 'c'. This 'c' block then connects to a larger lavender-colored horizontal bar labeled 'I(t)', which represents the input vector at time t. Below this bar, individual components I_1(t), I_2(t), ..., I_N(t) are shown as smaller lavender rectangles, indicating the N-dimensional input vector. 
- Module B (Reservoir Dynamics): Below the input layer, for each time step t, there is a gray rectangular container housing a sequence of N interconnected purple circular nodes labeled x_1(t), x_2(t), ..., x_N(t). These represent the reservoir state variables. Within each time step, the nodes are connected sequentially from left to right with solid arrows, indicating a feedforward propagation. Additionally, curved arrows connect earlier nodes to later ones within the same time step, suggesting recurrent or skip connections. Between consecutive time steps, curved arrows connect the last node of one time step (x_N(t)) to the first node of the next (x_1(t+1)), forming a temporal recurrence. 
- Module C (Multitask Readout Layer): At the bottom, for each time step t, a set of q lavender rectangular boxes labeled W_out,1, W_out,2, ..., W_out,q are shown. Each of these corresponds to a different task. They receive inputs from multiple nodes within the reservoir (specifically, from x_1(t), x_2(t), ..., x_N(t)) via downward arrows. Each W_out,k has a single downward arrow exiting it, indicating the output for that specific task at time t.

[3] Connections and Arrows: 
- From the top: External inputs z_1, z_2, ..., z_T enter the system at each time step, feeding into the 'c' blocks. 
- From 'c' to 'I(t)': A downward arrow connects each 'c' to its corresponding I(t) bar. 
- From I(t) to reservoir: Vertical arrows connect each component I_i(t) to the corresponding reservoir node x_i(t). 
- Within reservoir (Module B): Horizontal arrows connect x_i(t) to x_{i+1}(t) for i=1 to N-1. Curved arrows connect earlier nodes to later ones within the same time step (e.g., x_1(t) to x_3(t)). Temporal connections link x_N(t) to x_1(t+1), forming a cross-time-step recurrence. 
- From reservoir to readout (Module C): Multiple downward arrows connect each reservoir node x_i(t) to each of the W_out,k boxes, indicating that each readout task receives information from all reservoir states at time t. 
- From readout: Each W_out,k box outputs a single value via a downward arrow, representing the prediction or result for task k at time t.

The overall workflow proceeds as follows: At each time step t, an external input z_t is processed through a context module 'c', generating an input vector I(t). This vector drives the reservoir dynamics in Module B, where the state evolves both spatially (across nodes x_1 to x_N) and temporally (from t to t+1). Finally, the reservoir state at each time step is fed into the multitask readout layer C, where each task-specific weight matrix W_out,k produces an output for its respective task. The architecture is designed to handle sequential data over T time steps while supporting multiple parallel tasks.

The figure illustrates the internal structure of a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) unit, commonly used in sequence modeling for tasks such as query processing. The global layout is a rectangular block representing the LSTM cell at time step t+1, with inputs and outputs clearly labeled. Inputs include the previous cell state c_t, the current input vector v_{t+1}, and the previous hidden state h_t. Outputs are the updated cell state c_{t+1} and the new hidden state h_{t+1}. The cell is divided into three main functional components: the Input Gate, Forget Gate, and Output Gate, each represented by a green circle indicating an element-wise sum followed by a sigmoid or tanh activation function.

Visual modules and attributes: The green circles denote gate mechanisms (i_{t+1}, f_{t+1}, o_{t+1}) where the input, forget, and output gates compute gating signals using element-wise sums and activations. The yellow circle represents element-wise addition, specifically combining the gated input with the gated previous cell state to form c_{t+1}. The light blue circles with a dot symbol indicate element-wise multiplication operations. The φ symbols inside green circles represent nonlinear activation functions (sigmoid for gates, tanh for the cell state output). The red arrows signify matrix-vector product operations, while black arrows denote logical dependencies or data flow. The blue arrows represent element-wise multiplication. All input and output variables are enclosed in gray circles.

Connections and arrows: The diagram shows a clear data flow. The current input v_{t+1} and previous hidden state h_t feed into all three gates via red arrows (matrix-vector products). The previous cell state c_t also feeds into the forget gate and input gate via blue arrows (element-wise products). The forget gate f_{t+1} multiplies with c_t (blue arrow) to determine what to discard from the cell state. The input gate i_{t+1} multiplies with the tanh-activated input (φ applied to v_{t+1} and h_t) to determine what new information to store. These two results are added together (yellow circle) to produce the new cell state c_{t+1}. The output gate o_{t+1} modulates the tanh-activated c_{t+1} via element-wise multiplication (light blue circle) to produce the new hidden state h_{t+1}. The legend on the right clarifies the meaning of each arrow type and node color, ensuring the diagram’s operations are unambiguous. The overall structure reflects the LSTM’s ability to selectively remember or forget information over time, making it suitable for long-range dependencies in sequences.

The figure presents an end-to-end deep architecture for facial landmark detection, structured into four main components: (A) Spatial Resolution-Preserved Conv-Deconv Network, (B) Initialization Network, (C) Deep Recurrent Regression, and (D) Shape-Indexed Pooling (SIP). The global layout begins with an input image of size 256x256, which flows through a series of convolutional and deconvolutional layers in component (A). This network consists of five convolutional layers (conv1 to conv5) with decreasing feature map dimensions (256, 128, 64, 64, 64), followed by three deconvolutional layers (deconv6, deconv7, deconv8) that progressively restore spatial resolution, culminating in a 256x256 feature map from deconv7. The output of deconv7 is used in subsequent stages, while conv8 produces p-channel feature maps, each channel corresponding to a predicted facial keypoint, enabling the generation of an initial shape estimate S⁰.

Component (B), the Initialization Network, takes the conv8 output and applies a max-pooling operation to produce the initial landmark positions S⁰. This initialization feeds into component (C), the Deep Recurrent Regression module, which is depicted in an unrolled form to illustrate iterative refinement over K steps. Each step k involves an SIP layer that extracts shape-indexed features Fᵏ from the deconv7 feature map using the current shape estimate Sᵏ⁻¹. These features are concatenated with a memory cell Cᵏ⁻¹ from the previous LSTM state and fed into an LSTM unit to generate recurrent features F̃ᵏ. The concatenation of Fᵏ and F̃ᵏ is then passed to a regression module to compute the shape update ΔSᵏ, which is added to the previous shape Sᵏ⁻¹ to yield the refined shape Sᵏ. This process repeats for K iterations, producing increasingly accurate landmark predictions, visualized at the bottom with progressive refinement of red dot landmarks on the face.

Component (D) details the SIP mechanism: given the deconv7 feature map and a current shape Sᵏ, SIP uses the coordinates of each landmark to index into the feature map, extracting local feature vectors φᵢ for each point i. These are pooled via max-pooling to form a compact representation for each landmark, resulting in a feature vector Fᵏ. The SIP block is represented as a green rectangular box with multiple feature maps labeled s₁ to sₖ, each containing a blue square indicating the indexed region b, connected to a vertical stack of pooled features φᵢ.

Visual modules include rectangular blocks for convolutional/deconvolutional layers with labeled dimensions, blue rounded rectangles for LSTM units, gray boxes for SIP and regression, and circular nodes for feature vectors. Arrows indicate data flow: from input image → (A) → (B) → S⁰ → (C) → iterative refinement → final shape Sᴷ. Within (C), feedback loops connect the output Sᵏ back to SIP for the next iteration, and memory cells Cᵏ are passed forward between LSTMs. The bottom row shows the progression of landmark refinement from coarse to fine, with S = [(x₁,y₁), ..., (xₚ,yₚ)] denoting the final landmark set.

The figure illustrates the architecture for generating a joint image/text context vector through a recurrent neural network (RNN) framework initialized by a convolutional neural network (CNN) image embedding. The global layout is left-to-right, beginning with an image input (I) processed by a CNN module, represented as a trapezoidal block labeled 'CNN'. The output of this module, denoted as CNN(I), is shown in a yellow rectangular box and serves as the initial hidden state for the subsequent RNN sequence. This initialization is indicated by a dashed blue arrow labeled 'initialize' pointing from CNN(I) to the first RNN unit.

The RNN is unrolled across multiple time steps, depicted as three sequential RNN blocks (with ellipsis indicating intermediate steps), each corresponding to processing one word in the text sequence. Each RNN block contains internal components: a circular node representing the combination of the previous hidden state and current word input, leading to a computed hidden state (h̃_t), and a vertical rectangular block representing the actual hidden state vector h_t. In the first RNN block, h_{t=1} is explicitly set equal to CNN(I), shown in an orange rectangle. Subsequent blocks show h_{t=2}, h_{t=N} in red rectangles, indicating progression through the sequence. Each RNN block receives a word input (IN_word1, IN_word2, ..., IN_wordN-1) from below and produces an output (OUT_word2, OUT_word3, ..., OUT_wordN) above. Below the sequence of RNN blocks, dashed orange arrows connect each hidden state vector h_t (from t=1 to t=N) to a light green rectangular block labeled 'mean pooling'. This operation aggregates all hidden states across the sequence into a single vector. The output of mean pooling is a peach-colored rounded rectangle labeled h_IM:TEXT, identified as the 'joint image/text context vector'.

All RNN units share the same parameters, as stated in the caption, and are trained during the first round of training. The visual attributes include distinct colors: yellow for the CNN output, orange for the initial hidden state, red for subsequent hidden states, light green for the pooling layer, and peach for the final context vector. Shapes include trapezoids for CNN, rectangles for outputs and hidden states, circles for internal operations, and rounded rectangles for the final context vector. Text labels are placed adjacent to or inside these elements to denote their roles and mathematical representations.

The figure illustrates the computation of a convolution operation in a deep neural network (DNN), showing how input feature maps are processed by filters to produce output feature maps. The diagram is structured into two parallel horizontal workflows, each representing a different filter and its corresponding output location, arranged vertically to demonstrate the generality of the process.

[1] Global Layout and Structure:
The figure is divided into three main vertical sections: 'Filters' on the left, 'Input fmaps' in the center, and 'Output fmaps' on the right. Each section contains stacked rectangular blocks representing multiple channels or feature maps. The top row demonstrates the computation for the first output feature map, while the bottom row shows it for the N-th output feature map. [2] Visual Modules and Attributes:
In the 'Filters' section, each filter is represented as a stack of green rectangles with red borders, labeled with dimensions R (height), S (width), and C (number of channels). The top filter is marked with '1', and the bottom with 'M', indicating the filter index. In the 'Input fmaps' section, blue rectangles represent the input feature maps, with dimensions H (height), W (width), and C (channels). A red box highlights a receptive field of size R×S over the input maps, which corresponds to the spatial extent of the filter. In the 'Output fmaps' section, pink rectangles represent the output feature maps, with dimensions E (height), F (width), and M (number of output channels). [3] Connections and Arrows:

These lines converge at a single point in the output feature map, symbolizing the dot product between the filter weights and the input region. The figure illustrates the training architecture of a deep fine-grained explanation model designed to generate descriptive sentences for images, particularly emphasizing the integration of object category information and a dual-loss framework combining discriminative and relevance losses. The global layout is horizontally structured into three main sections: on the left, the Deep Finegrained Classifier processes an input image; in the center, an LSTM-based sequence generation module produces words sequentially; and on the right, two distinct loss components—Discriminative Loss and Relevance Loss—are computed to guide training.

In the left section, an input image (depicted as a red cardinal bird) is fed into a Compact Bilinear Classifier, represented by a blue trapezoid. This classifier outputs a 'Compact Bilinear Feature', which is then concatenated with the image category label ('Cardinal') via a 'Concat' node. This combined feature serves as the initial context for the central sequence generation module.

The central module consists of a stacked LSTM network. At each time step t, the LSTM receives the previous word (w_{t-1}) and the concatenated feature as inputs. The first word is initialized with '<SOS>' (start-of-sequence token). Each LSTM unit generates a probability distribution over the next word, denoted as p(w_t | w_{0:t-1}, I, C), where I is the image and C is the category. These probabilities are computed for each word in the generated sentence, such as 'a', 'red', 'bird', etc., up to the final word 'beak'. The target sentence, 'a bright red bird with an orange beak.', is shown at the bottom left for reference during training.

On the right side, two loss functions are computed. The Discriminative Loss, enclosed in a yellow box, evaluates the quality of the sampled sentence ('a red bird with black cheeks.') using a Sentence Classifier. The output of this classifier feeds into a Reward Function, which provides reinforcement learning feedback to optimize the model for generating discriminative descriptions.

Below it, the Relevance Loss, also in a yellow box, computes cross-entropy loss between the predicted word probabilities (p(w_1|w_0,I,C), p(w_2|w_0:1,I,C), ..., p(w_T|w_0:T-1,I,C)) and the ground truth target sentence. This ensures the generated sentence remains relevant and accurate.

Connections are drawn as solid black arrows indicating data flow: from the image through the classifier to the LSTM, from the LSTM outputs to both loss modules, and from the target sentence to the Relevance Loss for supervision. The figure emphasizes that the model uniquely integrates category information and employs reinforcement learning via the discriminative loss, distinguishing it from standard captioning models.
