The figure illustrates the architecture of Contour Guided MAE (Masked Autoencoder) for unsupervised vehicle re-identification. The global layout is divided into two main horizontal sections: the top section represents the main MAE framework, while the bottom section details the unsupervised feature learning module using contrastive learning with softening. The top section begins with an input image of a vehicle, which passes through a series of convolutional (conv), maxpooling, and distance transform operations, visualized as green, blue, and red blocks respectively. These processed features are then fed into a 'Contour Sorting' module, represented by an orange rectangle, which outputs a grid-like patch representation. This patch sequence enters the Encoder-Decoder structure enclosed in dashed boxes labeled '(Encoder)' and '(Decoder)'. Within the Encoder, the patch sequence undergoes 'Input Embedding', followed by addition with 'position encoding' (orange box), then passes through a Multi-Head Attention (MHA) block (peach-colored), normalization ('norm', light green), and a feed-forward network ('feed forward', light blue). The output is then passed to a 'Patch Fetch' module (yellow) before entering the Decoder. The Decoder mirrors the Encoder’s structure: position encoding, MHA, norm, feed forward, norm, and finally a 'Reshape' operation (beige) that reconstructs the original image. The bottom section shows a separate training loop for unsupervised feature learning. It starts with an 'Encoder' (light pink) processing 'trainset feature' (vertical bars). The output is clustered into 'ith cluster' and '(i-1)th cluster' (two overlapping 3D scatter plots with colored points), then passed through a 'softening' module (white box with scattered dots) to produce a 'feature dictionary' (vertical bars). A 'query feature' (horizontal bar) is compared against this dictionary, and the system computes a 'softening contrast loss' (blue box). An 'update' arrow from the loss back to the feature dictionary indicates parameter updates during training. A red double-headed arrow connects the main Encoder in the top section to the Encoder in the bottom section, indicating shared weights or feature extraction for both reconstruction and contrastive learning. The entire diagram uses consistent color-coding for modules: orange for position encoding, peach for MHA, light green for norm, light blue for feed forward, yellow for Patch Fetch, beige for Reshape, and light pink for the secondary Encoder. Text labels are placed directly on or near each module, and arrows indicate data flow direction.

The figure illustrates a complete pipeline for an open-world object detection framework built upon DDETR, incorporating two core innovations: Decoupled Objectness Learning and an Auxiliary Supervision Framework. The global layout is structured as a left-to-right data flow starting from an 'Input Image' on the far left, progressing through a deformable encoder, then branching into two parallel processing streams — one for label matching and guided learning, and another for auxiliary supervision — before converging into final output predictions.

On the top-left, the 'Input Image' (a real indoor scene) feeds into a 'Deformable Encoder', depicted as a rounded rectangle. From there, the process splits. The upper path leads to a large purple box labeled 'Label Matching', which contains a central orange block titled 'Hungarian Matching'. This module receives predicted object queries (represented by colored rectangles: dark gray for background, light blue for known objects, white for unknown objects) and matches them with ground-truth labels using bidirectional arrows. A legend clarifies color coding: light green/peach for known objects, dark gray for background, and white for unknown objects. Red arrows indicate label assignments for pseudo-unknowns, while black arrows denote assignments for known ground-truth. The Hungarian Matching outputs are fed into a green box labeled 'Auxiliary Supervision Framework', which is also connected via dashed green arrows to a separate, detailed inset on the top-right.

This inset, titled 'Auxiliary Supervision Framework', shows how SAM (Segment Anything Model) generates segmentation masks ('SAM Output') for the input image. These masks are used to compute region proposals (A_reg) and IoU scores, which, combined with predictions from an OWOD model (P_reg, P_obj), enable pseudo-labeling of unknown objects. The resulting 'Pseudo unknowns' are then fed back into the main pipeline.

The lower path from the Deformable Encoder leads to a large blue box titled 'Decoupled Objectness Learning'. Inside, this module visually represents the separation of learning objectives across decoder layers. On the left, a cluster of circles (representing object queries) is shown with blue arrows indicating 'Objectness learning' and red arrows for 'Classification learning'. The circles are color-coded: white for general objects, red for known objects, and green for unknown objects. A large gray arrow points right to a second stage where objectness learning occurs at 'Low-level' (blue star) and classification/regression at 'High-level' (red and green clusters). This emphasizes that objectness is learned early, while classification and regression follow.

Outputs from both pathways converge: P_obj (objectness), P_cls (classification), and P_reg (regression) are combined via a circular node (multiplication or fusion) to produce the final 'Output Results' on the far right. This output displays the original image with bounding boxes and labels — known objects like 'couch', 'chair', 'tv' with confidence scores, and numerous 'Unknown' labels for unannotated objects, demonstrating the open-world capability.

The entire diagram uses consistent visual elements: rounded rectangles for modules, colored rectangles for object queries, arrows for data flow, and dashed lines for auxiliary connections. Text annotations clarify roles, such as 'Guided Learning' beneath the Label Matching section, and legends for color coding. The design emphasizes modularity and the integration of external tools (SAM) for pseudo-supervision.

The figure illustrates an autoencoder-based generative network architecture, specifically designed for image-to-image translation tasks, such as converting a cat image into a dog image. The overall layout is horizontally oriented, with the input image on the far left and the output image on the far right, connected by a central processing pipeline divided into two main sections: Encoder (left, light blue background) and Decoder (right, light purple background). Above the main architecture, a detailed inset shows the structure of the 'SN ResBlock' (Spectral Normalized Residual Block), which is a core component used within both encoder and decoder stages.

[1] Global Layout and Structure:

The diagram follows a U-shaped architecture typical of autoencoders. The Encoder processes the input image through a series of downsampling layers, reducing spatial dimensions while increasing feature depth. The Decoder then reconstructs the image from the encoded representation, using upsampling layers to restore spatial resolution. A skip connection links corresponding layers between encoder and decoder, allowing direct flow of low-level features. The entire network is symmetrically structured around a bottleneck composed of nine consecutive SN ResBlocks, indicated by a bracketed label below the central part of the diagram.

[2] Visual Modules and Attributes:

Each module in the network is represented as a rectangular block with distinct colors and labels indicating its function. In the Encoder, the first layer is a pink 'Conv7*7' block, followed by a sequence of 'Conv3*3' blocks (pink), each paired with 'IN' (Instance Normalization, yellow), 'ReLU' (light blue), and 'FCA' (Feature Channel Attention, green) modules. These are repeated three times before transitioning into the bottleneck. The bottleneck consists of nine identical 'SN ResBlock' units, shown as large purple rectangles with a dashed outline and labeled 'SN ResBlock'.

In the Decoder, the process reverses: starting with 'Deconv3*3' (pink) blocks, each followed by 'IN' (yellow), 'ReLU' (light blue), and 'FCA' (green). This pattern repeats three times, culminating in a final 'Conv7*7' (pink) block followed by a 'Tanh' (light blue) activation to produce the output image.

The inset at the top, labeled 'SN ResBlock', details the internal structure: it begins with a 'SNconv3*3' (purple), followed by 'IN' (yellow) and 'ReLU' (light blue), then another 'Conv3*3' (pink) with 'IN' (yellow), and finally a skip connection (indicated by a circle with a plus sign) that adds the original input to the output of the second convolution, forming the residual connection.

[3] Connections and Arrows:

Arrows indicate the forward pass of data. From the input image, data flows rightward through the Encoder’s layers. After the third 'Conv3*3' + FCA block, the signal enters the bottleneck of nine SN ResBlocks. From the last SN ResBlock, the signal proceeds to the Decoder. Skip connections are drawn as horizontal lines from each encoder block (after ReLU) to the corresponding decoder block (before Deconv3*3), enabling feature reuse. The final output is generated after the Tanh activation, producing the translated image (e.g., a dog from a cat).

The figure caption states: 'SN Residual block. The SN residual block can enhance the stability of training and assist the generator to extract more complex features.' This highlights the role of the SN ResBlock in improving training stability and feature extraction capability.

The figure illustrates a cross-stream contrastive learning framework for skeleton-based action recognition. The global layout is horizontally structured, progressing from left to right: input data streams, feature encoding, contrastive learning modules, and final positive feature transformation. On the far left, two distinct data streams are shown: Stream-u, represented by orange wavy lines indicating motion trajectories, and Stream-v, depicted as a 3D skeletal structure with orange dots connected by lines, representing joint positions. Both streams undergo augmentation before being fed into separate encoder branches.

Each stream has two parallel encoder paths: Query Encoder and Key Encoder. For Stream-u, both encoders are shaded blue; for Stream-v, they are shaded yellow. Each encoder outputs an intermediate feature representation (h_q^u, h_k^u for Stream-u; h_q^v, h_k^v for Stream-v), followed by a projected feature vector (z_q^u, z_k^u, etc.). These projected features are used for contrastive learning.

The central part of the diagram contains four dashed rectangular boxes representing contrastive learning objectives. Two are labeled 'Intra-Stream Correspondence' with loss term L_intra: one for Stream-u (blue bars, M_u) and one for Stream-v (yellow bars, M_v). These compare features within the same stream. Two additional boxes labeled 'Inter-Stream Correspondence' with loss term L_inter connect features across streams: one linking Stream-u’s key features to Stream-v’s query features (M_v, yellow bars), and another linking Stream-v’s key features to Stream-u’s query features (M_u, blue bars). These enforce correspondence between different streams.

Gradient backpropagation arrows (dashed black lines) flow backward from the loss modules to the encoders, indicating the training signal. A large blue arrow points from the contrastive learning section to the rightmost module titled 'Positive Feature Transformation'. This module takes original positive pairs (z_q and z_k) as input, applies a 'Mixup' operation (shown as an orange box), and outputs synthetic positive pairs (ẑ_q and ẑ_k). The synthetic features are visually distinguished by mixed color shades (light and dark blue), indicating feature blending. This step aims to enhance feature robustness by generating diverse positive samples.

Text labels clearly identify each component: encoders, feature vectors, loss functions, and transformation steps. The overall workflow follows a logical sequence: data input → augmentation → dual-branch encoding → intra- and inter-stream contrastive learning → gradient update → positive pair synthesis via Mixup. The diagram effectively conveys a multi-stream, self-supervised learning pipeline designed to improve generalization through cross-modal correspondence and synthetic data generation.

The figure illustrates the standard U-Net architecture commonly used in nnU-Net, depicted as a symmetric encoder-decoder structure with skip connections. The global layout is horizontally oriented, with the input on the left and output on the right, forming a U-shape. The encoder (left half) progressively reduces spatial dimensions while increasing feature channel depth, followed by the decoder (right half) which upsamples features back to the original resolution. Skip connections are represented by dotted horizontal lines linking corresponding layers between encoder and decoder, enabling feature reuse.

Visual modules include blue rectangles labeled with numbers (e.g., 32, 64, 128, 256, 320) representing convolutional layers; orange rectangles (labeled 128, 64, 32) denote transpose convolution layers used for upsampling; a single light cyan rectangle at the end represents the classification layer; and pink circles indicate concatenation blocks where features from skip connections are merged with upsampled features. All rectangles are uniform in size and aligned vertically within each stage, with arrows indicating forward flow. The numbers inside the rectangles correspond to the number of feature channels in each layer.

Connections and arrows show the data flow: solid black arrows indicate sequential processing within the encoder and decoder paths. In the encoder, each stage typically consists of two convolutional layers followed by a downsampling step (implied by the vertical drop to the next stage). The decoder mirrors this with two convolutional layers followed by a transpose convolution layer for upsampling. At each level of the decoder, a pink concatenation block merges the upsampled features with the corresponding features from the encoder via a dotted line, preserving spatial context. The final output path includes three layers: two convolutional layers (blue, 32 channels) followed by a classification layer (light cyan, 32 channels), producing the final output. The legend on the bottom right explicitly defines the color coding: blue for convolutional layers, orange for transpose convolutions, light cyan for classification, and pink for concatenation blocks.

The figure presents an overview of the active learning pipeline for round t (where t > 0) in a proposed semi-supervised learning framework. The global layout is structured horizontally into four main stages, each enclosed in a colored box: supervised training (1) in yellow, pseudo-labeling (2) in light orange, semi-supervised training (3) in pink, and acquisition (4) in light blue. These stages are fed by the 'round t dataset', represented on the left by two green boxes labeled L_t (labeled data) and U_t (unlabeled data), and output to the 'round t+1 dataset' on the right, also in green, with updated L_{t+1} and U_{t+1}. Above the main pipeline, a separate pre-training stage is shown in light gray, using the 'round 0 dataset' (green box with L_0 and U_0) to train a backbone via SSL (self-supervised learning), which initializes subsequent rounds.

In the first stage, supervised training (1), the labeled data L_t is used to train M=3 independent models, denoted as f_{t1}, f_{t2}, f_{t3}, each represented as a white parallelogram. These models are trained for K+1-way classification. In the second stage, pseudo-labeling (2), the outputs of these three models are combined through an ensemble prediction (white triangle) to generate pseudo-labels for the unlabeled set U_t, stored in a white rectangle labeled 'pseudo-labels of U_t'.

In the third stage, semi-supervised training (3), both the original labeled data L_t and the newly generated pseudo-labeled data from U_t are used to retrain the same M=3 models, now denoted as f'_{t1}, f'_{t2}, f'_{t3}, again represented as white parallelograms. These models are initialized using the weights from the previous round's models (indicated by dashed lines labeled 'init').

In the fourth stage, acquisition (4), the outputs of the three retrained models f'_{t1}, f'_{t2}, f'_{t3} are again combined via ensemble prediction (white triangle) to feed an acquisition function (white triangle). This function selects a subset of the unlabeled data, forming the 'acquired set' (white rectangle), which is then annotated (as indicated by the arrow labeled 'annotation') to become part of the next round’s labeled data L_{t+1}, while the remaining unselected data becomes U_{t+1}.

A blue box labeled 'used for testing' points upward from the semi-supervised training stage, indicating that a single model (not shown explicitly) is used for final K-way classification on inliers during testing, distinct from the ensemble-based internal processes. The figure emphasizes that ensembles are only used internally for pseudo-labeling and acquisition, not for final testing. The entire process is iterative, with each round updating the dataset for the next iteration.

The figure illustrates the P4R framework, a two-step method for learning enhanced item profile representations using large language models (LLMs) and aligning them with graph neural network (GNN)-based collaborative filtering representations for recommendation tasks. The overall layout is divided into two main stages: Step 1: Profile Representation Learning and Step 2: GNN-based Alignment, separated by dashed boundaries. Above these steps, two example prompt-response pairs are shown: one gray box describes the assistant’s role in analyzing user preferences for a business, and a green box provides an example output including summarization, user preferences, and recommendation reasoning for 'Sugar Bowl' in Scottsdale, AZ.

In Step 1, contextual information about an item—such as name, categories, city/state, average ratings, review counts, and coordinates—is input into a prompt. This prompt is fed into a cloud-shaped module labeled 'LLMs Llama2(7B)', which generates a structured profile containing three components: Summarization, User Preferences, and Recommendation Reasoning. These generated profiles are then encoded using a BERT model (110M parameters), followed by a fully connected (FC) layer, producing dense embeddings. These embeddings serve as the learned profile representation.

Step 2 involves GNN-based alignment. The embeddings from Step 1 are integrated into a trainable graph structure composed of nodes representing users and items. A designed GNN processes this graph, performing message passing between nodes. For each node, the GNN aggregates features from its neighbors using a 'Normalized Sum' operation, weighted by learnable parameters α and β. The aggregation combines embeddings from previous layers (e.g., e_u^(l-1) for users, e_i^(l-1) for items) with current layer embeddings (e_i^k, e_u^k). The resulting updated embeddings are then used for downstream recommendation tasks.

On the left side, under 'RS Tasks', a simplified diagram shows multiple users leading to predictions for different items, represented by colored circles (gray, yellow, pink). Dashed arrows indicate the flow of information from the GNN to the prediction module. The entire framework is trained end-to-end, aligning the LLM-generated textual profiles with the GNN-based collaborative filtering representations to improve recommendation accuracy.

The figure presents an overview of the CatVTON method, a lightweight image-to-image translation framework for virtual try-on that operates without requiring additional conditions such as pose or parsing maps. The global layout is structured as a left-to-right pipeline: input images on the left, processed through an encoder, then a denoising UNet with transformer blocks, followed by a decoder to produce the final output. The top-left corner shows two input images — a target person and a garment image — which are concatenated in the spatial dimension using a circular symbol labeled 'C' (as defined in the legend), forming a composite input. A 10% dropout is applied to the garment image before concatenation. This concatenated image is fed into a VAE Encoder, marked with a snowflake icon indicating it is frozen (non-trainable). The encoder outputs two representations: one mask-free and one mask-based, both shown as pairs of images with the target person and garment. These are then combined via channel-wise concatenation (indicated by a circle with a dot, per legend) and passed into the Denoising UNet. The Denoising UNet is depicted as a series of alternating light blue (ResNet Blocks, frozen) and light orange (Transformer Blocks, learnable) rectangular modules arranged in a U-shaped structure. Each Transformer Block contains three components: Self Attention (light orange, marked with a flame icon for learnable), Cross Attention (light gray, receiving 'Text Embed' input but not used in this setup), and FFN (Feed-Forward Network, light blue, marked with a snowflake for frozen). A dashed arrow labeled 'Skip Cross Attn' bypasses the Cross Attention layer, indicating it is omitted from the model. The output of the Denoising UNet is split in space (indicated by scissors icon) to separate the person and garment regions, then passed to a VAE Decoder (also frozen, marked with snowflake) to reconstruct the final try-on image. The legend on the right clarifies symbols: 'C' for concatenate in space, 'O' for concatenate in channel, scissors for split in space, flame for learnable, snowflake for frozen, light blue squares for ResNet Blocks, and light orange for Transformer Blocks. The caption emphasizes that only self-attention parameters are learnable, enabling efficient training and inference with minimal trainable parameters.

The figure illustrates the architecture of the proposed Multi-modal Intermediate Feature Interaction AutoEncoder (MIFI-AE), divided into encoding and decoding components. The global layout is structured horizontally from left to right, beginning with input data on the far left and progressing through encoding, feature interaction, decoding, and output stages. The diagram is segmented into two main regions: (a) the encoding path, shaded light blue, and (b) the decoding path, shaded light pink. A central module labeled 'CMIFM' (Cross-Modal Intermediate Feature Module) connects the encoding outputs with tabular data for multimodal fusion. Below the main pipeline, a legend defines symbols used: bidirectional arrows for loss computation, ⊕ for element-wise addition, ⊗ for concatenation, and ⊗ for mask multiplication.

In the encoding section (a), the input consists of an 'Original CT' image and a 'GTV-T' mask, which are multiplied via mask multiplication (⊗) before entering the encoder. The first layer is a Conv3D block followed by MaxPool. This is followed by three sequential Residual Blocks, each producing feature maps F₁, F₂, and F₃. These features are simultaneously fed into AdaAvgPool layers to generate downsampled representations F₁_img, F₂_img, and F₃_img. All three feature maps F₁, F₂, F₃ are also sent upward to the MFFSM (Multi-Feature Fusion and Selection Module), a purple rectangular box at the top, which outputs F₁_out, F₂_out, and F₃_out. The encoding continues with a Swin Block processing F₃ to produce F₄, which then enters the decoding path.

The decoding section (b) begins with F₄ being processed through a TansConv3D layer, followed by a Residual Block to generate F₅. This is followed by another TansConv3D layer and Residual Block to produce F₆. Each of these decoding steps receives skip connections from the corresponding F₁_out, F₂_out, and F₃_out outputs from MFFSM. The final decoding stage includes a TansConv3D layer leading to the 'Output Feature Map'.

The CMIFM module, located centrally below the encoding path, receives F₁_img, F₂_img, F₃_img as inputs and combines them into F_img. It also receives 'Tabular data', represented as a table with columns like Patient No., PathTN Mstage, and Strength, which is transformed via T₀ into F_tab. F_img and F_tab are concatenated (⊕) and passed through an FC Layer to produce a 'Risk Score'. This risk score is linked to 'Survival data' via the loss function ℒ_Surv. Additionally, F_img and F_tab are connected via a bidirectional arrow labeled ℒ_Align, indicating alignment loss computation between modalities.

A detailed inset on the bottom right shows the internal structure of the TansConv3D module. It consists of a series of convolutional blocks: a 1×1×1 convolution followed by BatchNorm+ReLU, then a 3×3×3 convolution with BatchNorm+ReLU, and finally another 1×1×1 convolution with BatchNorm+ReLU. This sequence is repeated n−1 times, with the outputs summed together via element-wise addition (⊕) before being passed forward.

Loss functions are indicated at the top: ℒ_Recon connects the original CT input to the Output Feature Map, representing reconstruction loss. The entire pipeline integrates multimodal data—image, tabular, and survival—through feature fusion and alignment, enabling both reconstruction and survival prediction tasks.

The figure presents an overview of the GETNext model, a deep learning framework for next POI (Point of Interest) prediction, structured into three main components: Generic Movement Learning, Contextual Embeddings, and Encoder-Decoder. The global layout is left-to-right, with data flowing from historical check-in records on the top-left through various processing modules to final predictions and loss computation at the bottom-right.

On the far left, under 'Generic Movement Learning', historical check-in records (a table with columns Idx, User, POI, Time) feed into a 'Trajectory Flow Map'—a directed graph of blue nodes representing POIs with edges indicating transitions and a 'Popularity' label. This map is processed by a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) stack consisting of three green 'GCN Layer' blocks, separated by a red 'Dropout' layer. The output of the GCN is labeled 'POI Embeddings'. A separate 'Transition Attention Module' also receives input from the Trajectory Flow Map and outputs a 'Probability Map', which later feeds into the final prediction stage.

In the center, the 'Contextual Embeddings' module processes the 'Input Trajectory' (a sequence q₁, q₂, ..., qₜ₋₁). This module has three parallel embedding paths: 'User Embedding layer' (blue) produces 'User Embeddings' (yellow), 'Category Embedding layer' (blue) produces 'Category Embeddings' (yellow), and 'Time2Vec' (a sub-module with two 'Linear' layers, one followed by 'Sin activation', then concatenated) generates 'Time Embeddings' (yellow). Each pair of embeddings (User & Category, and Category & Time) is fused via a 'Fusion' block (white), and the results are concatenated via a green 'Concat' node to form the 'Encoded Sequence' (blue).

On the right, the 'Encoder-Decoder' component, labeled 'Transformer Layers', takes the 'Encoded Sequence' as input. It consists of stacked transformer blocks, each containing a blue 'Multi-head Self-Attention' layer, followed by a red 'Dropout', then a gray 'Add&Norm' layer; this is followed by a green 'Feed-forward' layer, another red 'Dropout', and a final 'Add&Norm'. The output of the encoder-decoder is split into three heads: 'POI Head', 'Time Head', and 'Category Head' (all white boxes). These heads produce predictions for 'POI', 'Time', and 'Category' (gray boxes). The 'Probability Map' from the left side is combined with the 'POI' prediction via a circular fusion symbol (blue). All three predictions are then fed into a final 'Loss' (red box) for training.

The visual style uses dashed blue borders to group major modules, with color-coded blocks: blue for input/layer names, yellow for embedding outputs, green for operations like Concat and GCN, red for Dropout and Loss, and gray for final outputs and Add&Norm. Arrows indicate data flow, with solid lines for direct connections and a curved line from the Probability Map to the POI prediction. The diagram is self-contained, with all necessary components and their interconnections clearly shown.

The figure illustrates a hybrid deep learning architecture combining a pre-trained DenseNet subnetwork with a multi-prototype deep capsule network. The global layout is divided into two main horizontal sections: the upper section represents the DenseNet feature extraction module, and the lower section depicts the capsule network architecture. A blue arrow connects the output of the DenseNet to the input of the capsule network, indicating the flow of features.

In the upper section, labeled 'Pre-trained DenseNet subnetwork', an input image (shown as a hamster photo) is processed through a sequence of layers. First, a 7×7 convolutional layer with Batch Normalization and ReLU activation (colored orange) produces 64 feature maps. This is followed by a 2×2 max pooling layer (pink), which reduces spatial dimensions. The resulting feature maps (58×58×64) feed into multiple dense blocks, represented by stacked beige rectangular layers. Each dense block contains a series of connected gray circles symbolizing dense connections, with 'Dense Block 1' explicitly labeled in yellow. The entire block structure is repeated 'n' times, as indicated below the block. The final output from this subnetwork is a set of DenseNet feature maps of size 28×28×32, shown as a yellow rectangular stack on the right.

The lower section details the capsule network. It begins with a 3D gray block labeled 'ReLU Conv1', which processes the incoming DenseNet features. From this, a capsule layer ('Caps 1') is formed, depicted as a gray cube with a blue square inside. The capsules are arranged in a grid, with each capsule represented as a small colored rectangle (blue, green, yellow) containing an eye-like icon to denote prototype features. These capsules are organized into groups: the first group has 'p' capsules with vectors v^l_{1,1} to v^l_{1,|o^l_1|}, the second group has 'p' capsules with vectors v^l_{p,1} to v^l_{p,|o^l_p|}, and so on up to 'nobj' groups. Each group's capsules are connected via a weight matrix W_ij = [8 × 12], and the total number of capsules in layer l is denoted as n^l = Σ rows(v^l_p).

These capsules are then routed to a higher-level capsule layer, 'Final Caps', which consists of 16 capsules (indicated above the column). The capsules here are similarly colored and structured, with vectors v^L_{1,1} to v^L_{c,|o^L_c|}. The routing weights between layers are specified as W_ij = [12 × 16]. The final output is computed as the L2 norm of the capsule vectors, ||L_2||, and the total number of capsules in the final layer is given by n^k = Σ_{k=1}^c |o_k|. The entire capsule network is designed to learn hierarchical representations using dynamic routing, with the final capsule outputs representing the presence and properties of objects or parts in the image.

The figure presents the overall framework of the proposed MLMC (Meta Learning based Multi-scale Kernel Convolution) method, structured into four main horizontal sections, each representing a distinct component or stage of the algorithm. The entire diagram is organized as a multi-stage pipeline with iterative processes, clearly demarcated by dashed lines and labeled iterations.

[1] Global Layout and Structure:
The figure is vertically divided into four major blocks: (i) Meta Learning based Alternating Optimization (MLAO), (ii) Overall Workflow of MLMC, (iii) Markov Chain Monte Carlo Kernel Approximation (MCKA), and (iv) an upper section detailing the inner optimization loop within MLAO. Each block spans horizontally across multiple iterations, indicated by dotted vertical separators and labels such as '1st iteration', 'p-th iteration', 'q-th iteration', etc. The topmost section illustrates the alternating optimization process between kernel parameters and image parameters, while the bottom section details the MCKA module used for kernel sampling. The middle section integrates these components into the full MLMC workflow.

[2] Visual Modules and Attributes:
- In the top section (MLAO inner loop), rectangular boxes represent parameters or modules: φ_k^q,i_ML (light blue), φ_x^p,i (salmon), L_RE-n (red), L_meta^q (light blue), and G_k/G_x (black text). The loss terms are shown as red rectangles with gradients (∇φ) feeding back into parameter updates. Dashed lines indicate iterative progression.
- The second section (MLAO) shows a sequence of φ_x updates (salmon boxes) and φ_k^q,i_ML updates (light blue), with meta-losses L_meta^q (light blue) computed and used to update φ_k via gradient descent. The process runs from input to output over Q iterations.
- The third section (Overall Workflow of MLMC) shows the integration of MCKA and MLAO. Input includes {k_i^l}_{i=1}^L (blue box), z_k (black dot), and φ_k^l_MC (blue box). These feed into MCKA, which outputs φ_k^l_ML (light blue), then into MLAO, which outputs φ_x^l (salmon). After I iterations, final outputs x (image) and k (kernel heatmap) are produced. The MCKA module is represented by a gray rectangle, MLAO by a beige rectangle.
- The bottom section (MCKA) details the kernel approximation process. It starts with φ_k^l,i_MC (blue) and z_k (black dot), generating sampled kernels {k_g^{l,i}}_{g=1}^T (small heatmaps). These are fed into G_k(z_k, φ_k^l,i_MC) to compute L_MC (light blue), whose gradient updates φ_k^l,i_MC. This repeats over L iterations, culminating in φ_k^l_ML (output).

[3] Connections and Arrows:
Arrows indicate data flow and parameter updates. Solid arrows show forward propagation: e.g., from φ_k^q,i_ML to G_k, from G_k to L_RE-n, and from φ_x to G_x. Feedback loops are shown via downward arrows from loss terms (e.g., ∇φ_k^q,i L_meta^q) to parameter boxes, indicating gradient-based updates. Dotted lines separate iterations and denote temporal progression. In the MCKA section, arrows connect sampled kernels to G_k, then to L_MC, and finally to the parameter update. The overall workflow connects MCKA output to MLAO input, and MLAO output to the final reconstruction x and kernel k.

The diagram uses color coding consistently: light blue for kernel-related parameters (φ_k), salmon for image parameters (φ_x), red for reconstruction losses (L_RE-n), and light blue again for meta-losses (L_meta). Heatmap icons represent kernel samples. Text labels specify mathematical expressions like G_k(z_k, φ_k^q,i_ML) and gradients ∇φ_k^q,i L_meta^q. The structure emphasizes iterative refinement and alternating optimization between kernel and image parameters, with MCKA providing kernel diversity through sampling.

The figure illustrates a multi-stage training and inference framework for learning representations from Screening Mammography (SM) images by leveraging knowledge from Full-Field Digital Mammography (FFDM) images. The diagram is divided into two main sections: 'Training' on the left, subdivided into three stages (Stage I, Stage II, Stage III), and 'Inference' on the right.

[1] Global Layout and Structure:

The layout is horizontally segmented into four vertical columns: Stage I, Stage II, Stage III under the 'Training' header, followed by the 'Inference' section. Each stage shows a flow from input images through processing modules to output detections. Dotted vertical lines separate the training stages. The inference section mirrors the final stage of training but uses only SM images. A legend at the bottom explains visual cues: solid-colored boxes indicate components trained end-to-end, diagonally striped boxes denote pre-trained and frozen components, and a circle with a plus sign represents concatenation along the channel axis.

[2] Visual Modules and Attributes:

In Stage I, SM Images feed into a light blue box labeled 'A', producing feature representation h_SM, which is passed to a light blue trapezoid labeled 'Predictor'. Similarly, FFDM Images go into a pink box labeled 'C', yielding h_FFDM, fed into a pink Predictor. Both predictors output detection results with bounding box coordinates and class labels (Benign/Malignant).

In Stage II, SM Images enter a light green box 'B' (trained end-to-end), generating h'_SM, which passes through a green 'Projector' module to produce z'_SM. FFDM Images go into a red-striped box 'C' (pre-trained/frozen), producing h_FFDM. A loss term L_sim(z'_SM, h_FFDM) is computed between these representations, indicating a contrastive or alignment objective.

In Stage III, SM Images are processed by both box 'A' (light blue, trained end-to-end) and box 'B' (light green with diagonal stripes, pre-trained/frozen), producing h_SM and h'_SM respectively. These features are concatenated via the ⊕ symbol to form h_FUSED, which feeds into an orange trapezoid 'Predictor' to yield detections.

In Inference, SM Images are processed by both box 'A' (light blue, diagonally striped, pre-trained/frozen) and box 'B' (light green, diagonally striped, pre-trained/frozen), producing h_SM and h'_SM. These are concatenated to form h_FUSED, which is processed by an orange trapezoid 'Predictor' to generate final detections.

All predictors are depicted as trapezoids, and all feature representations are shown in rounded rectangles. The color coding consistently indicates training status: solid colors for end-to-end training, striped patterns for pre-trained/frozen modules.

[3] Connections and Arrows:

Arrows indicate data flow direction. From inputs (SM/FFDM Images) to modules (A, B, C), then to intermediate features (h_SM, h_FFDM, h'_SM, z'_SM), followed by concatenation (⊕) to form h_FUSED, and finally to the Predictor for detections. In Stage II, a bidirectional arrow connects z'_SM and h_FFDM to the loss function L_sim, indicating the alignment objective. All connections are unidirectional except for this feedback-like loss computation. The inference path replicates the fusion logic of Stage III but uses only SM images and pre-trained modules.

The figure presents a side-by-side comparison of two self-attention architectures: (a) Temporal Difference Self-Attention (TDSA) and (b) Simplified Spiking Self-Attention (S3A). The global layout consists of two vertically aligned diagrams, each illustrating a distinct computational pipeline for processing video tokens. Both diagrams share a similar top-down flow, starting from input token representations, passing through feature extraction modules, generating query (Q), key (K), and value (V) sequences, and finally computing attention outputs.

In diagram (a), the input is labeled 'Continuous Tube Tokens X', represented by a 3D grid of green cubes. These tokens are processed through three parallel branches: two yellow rectangular blocks labeled 'TDC' (Temporal Difference Convolution) and one gray block labeled 'Conv 3D'. Each branch feeds into a white rounded rectangle labeled 'Vid2Seq', producing Q, K, and V respectively. The outputs are visualized as grids of colored squares—peach for Q, blue for K, and green for V—arranged in N rows and D columns. The Q and K matrices are transposed and fed into a dot product operation (black circle), followed by a Softmax layer. The resulting N×N attention map is then multiplied with the V matrix (another dot product) to produce the final N×D output.

Diagram (b) shows S3A, which uses 'Binary Spike Tube Tokens S' as input, depicted similarly but with red spiking waveforms inside some cubes. Here, only the leftmost TDC module is used for Q computation; the other two branches (TDC and Conv 3D) are used for V and K, respectively. Each branch includes a spiking neuron symbol (red waveform in a circle) before Vid2Seq, indicating binary spike processing. The resulting Q, K, and V matrices are shown with spiking waveforms embedded within their colored squares. The attention mechanism differs significantly: instead of matrix multiplication, it uses a Hadamard product (star symbol) between Q and K to create an element-wise mask, followed by column summation (Σ symbol) and a column mask (black square) applied to V. This produces the final N×D output.

The bottom legend defines symbols: black circle = dot product, black square = column mask, star = Hadamard product (element-wise mask), and red waveform in circle = spiking neuron. The figure emphasizes computational efficiency: TDSA requires 2N²D multiply-and-accumulate operations due to continuous values and matrix multiplication, while S3A reduces this to fND accumulations, where f is the non-zero ratio (typically <0.06) after masking, leveraging binary spikes and addition-only operations.

The output of this stage is a grid of red square tiles, indicating BEV feature maps.

These BEV features enter the 'BEV Encoder' section, divided into 'Backbone' and 'Neck'. The Backbone consists of three stacked red tile grids connected vertically by upward-pointing red arrows labeled 'Resnet Block', indicating progressive feature extraction with residual connections. The Neck includes a central crop operation (marked by a brown square icon) applied to one of the feature levels, followed by a concatenation step (indicated by a small circle connecting two feature maps), and a final feature map that branches out to two task-specific heads.

The first branch leads to the 'Task-special Head' for 'Occupancy Prediction', highlighted in pink. It includes an 'MC Head' (multi-convolution head) in a green rounded rectangle, followed by a sequence of red tile grids, then a yellow trapezoidal block representing a temporal fusion module (optional, activated by a red switch as per caption), and finally a stack of light blue cubes symbolizing a 3D convolutional or upsampling layer. The second branch leads to the '3D Object Detection' head, containing a 'CenterPoint Head' in a gray rounded rectangle. The legend in the upper right corner defines three icons: a red circle with a dot for 'Upsample', a brown square for 'Central Crop', and a red upward arrow for 'Resnet Block'. The figure presents a comparative architectural overview of four distinct point cloud processing methods: (a) PointMLP, (b) PointMAE, (c) PointMamba, and (d) PointRWKV, arranged in a 2x2 grid layout separated by dashed lines. Each quadrant illustrates the data flow from input point cloud to prediction head, emphasizing structural differences and core modules.

In (a) PointMLP, the input 'Point Cloud' (visually represented as a red sketched guitar) undergoes 'Geometric Affine' transformation (blue rectangle), followed by 'Token Embedding' (orange rectangle). The output feeds into a 'Residual Point Block' (gray box), which contains an MLP layer (yellow), Batch Normalization (BN, yellow), two ReLU activations (gray), and a skip connection via element-wise addition (circle with plus sign). This block outputs to a 'Prediction Head' (light blue rectangle).

In (b) PointMAE, the 'Point Cloud' is first subjected to 'Masking' (indicated by a row of circles—some filled with red texture, others striped or empty—representing masked/unmasked points). The masked points proceed to 'Token Embedding' (orange), then enter a 'Transformer Block' (gray box) composed of three stacked encoders (Encoder 1–3, light blue) and two decoders (Decoder 1–2, light green). The final output connects to the 'Prediction Head' (light blue).

In (c) PointMamba, the 'Point Cloud' (red guitar) is processed through 'Token Embedding' (orange), then a 'Reordering Strategy' (green rectangle). The reordered tokens enter a 'Mamba Block' (gray box) repeated L times (indicated by '×L'). Inside, a 'Linear' layer (light green) feeds into a 'SSM' (State Space Model, light blue) with a sigmoid activation (σ), followed by a 'Conv' layer (light blue). Two parallel 'Linear' layers (light green) connect to the SSM and Conv, with one path including a multiplication operation (⊗) and the other a σ activation. The combined output goes to the 'Prediction Head' (light blue).

In (d) PointRWKV, the 'Point Cloud' (red guitar) is split into 'Multi-scale Points' (three blue sketched guitars of decreasing density), which are then passed through 'Token Embedding' (orange). These embeddings feed into a 'PRWKV Block' (gray box), also repeated L times ('×L'). The block includes 'Local Merging' (blue), 'Spatial Mixing' (light green), and 'Channel Mixing' (yellow), with connections forming a hierarchical structure: spatial mixing feeds into channel mixing, which combines with local merging via element-wise addition (circle with plus sign), and the result passes through a circular node labeled 'C' before reaching the 'Prediction Head' (light blue).

All subfigures share a consistent visual style: point clouds are sketched guitars; embedding layers are orange; prediction heads are light blue; core blocks are gray; and internal operations use colored rectangles (yellow for MLP, light blue for Conv/SSM/Encoders, light green for Linear/Decoders/Spatial Mixing). Arrows indicate forward data flow, with skip connections shown as curved lines. The figure highlights how PointRWKV uniquely integrates multi-scale features and efficient linear-complexity modeling via PRWKV blocks, contrasting with MLP, Transformer, and Mamba-based approaches.

The figure presents an architectural overview of the MegaFusion framework, divided into three main parts: (a) the Truncate and Relay strategy and inference pipeline, (b) the incorporation of dilated convolutions to enhance receptive fields, and (c) the impact of noise scheduling across different resolutions.

Part (a) illustrates a multi-stage inference pipeline using the Truncate and Relay strategy. It begins with random noise input, which is processed through a Diffusion UNet composed of alternating green blocks representing standard convolution layers and blue blocks representing dilated convolution layers. After processing, the output passes through a yellow 'Truncate' module followed by a red-dashed blue box labeled 'D', representing the VAE decoder. This produces a low-resolution image denoted as x̂₁^t₁. An upsampler then enhances this to a higher-resolution image x̂₂^t₁. In the next stage, the output from the previous stage is fed into a blue-dashed box labeled 'ε', representing the VAE encoder, followed by a yellow 'Relay' module that adds current noise. This combined signal enters another Diffusion UNet, again with standard and dilated convolutions, followed by Truncate and D modules, yielding x̂₂^t₂. A subsequent upsampler generates x̂₃^t₂. The final stage repeats the Relay and Diffusion UNet process, leading to the final output x₀³. The legend clarifies that 'Truncate' denotes one-step denoising, 'Relay' adds current noise, 'ε' is the VAE encoder, 'D' is the VAE decoder, light green blocks are standard convolutions, and dark blue blocks are dilated convolutions.

Part (b), titled 'Incorporated dilated convolution', compares three methods: Stable Diffusion, MegaFusion, and MegaFusion-Dilated. Each shows two rows of images depicting rabbits on grass. The top row displays intermediate noisy states with highlighted receptive fields (yellow grids). In Stable Diffusion, the receptive field is small, leading to object replication and poor detail. MegaFusion improves this slightly, but MegaFusion-Dilated uses larger, spaced-out receptive fields (due to dilated convolutions), resulting in clearer, more coherent images with better semantic accuracy and fewer artifacts.

Part (c), titled 'Noise scheduler affects images differently', demonstrates how noise levels at different timesteps (t=0, 100, 200, 300, 400) affect images at three resolutions: original, higher, and higher with re-scheduled noise. At original resolution, noise decreases gradually and predictably. At higher resolution without rescheduling, noise remains too high even at later timesteps, causing blurry or distorted outputs. With noise re-scheduling, the noise level at higher resolution matches that of the original resolution, producing cleaner, more stable results across all timesteps.

The Guided LDM generates a sequence of images: an 'Original' image, followed by 'Intermediate Steps', and finally a 'Counterfactual' image, all depicted as small square skin lesion images. Section 2, 'Semantic Space Disentanglement', shows the training of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE). Between them lies a vertical stack of white circles representing the 'Disentangled Semantic Space'. The reconstructed image is output by the decoder and compared to the original via a loss function labeled 'L_VAE', forming a feedback loop to train the model. Section 3, 'Discovery of Relevant Concepts', uses the 'Trained VAE' on a separate 'ISIC Validation' dataset (another blue database icon). The figure presents an overview of the NeRF2Points method for generating a complete street-view point cloud from RGB sequences, depth maps, and normal vectors using NeRF-based modeling. The global layout is divided into two main vertical sections: the left side shows input data streams, while the right side illustrates the processing pipeline and output. On the left, three parallel sequences—labeled 'DEPTH' (color gradient cubes), 'NORMAL' (gray-scale images), and 'RGB-Seq' (color images)—are shown as stacked 3D blocks representing sequential frames. These inputs are combined with camera poses (depicted as a panoramic street view image) and fed into two separate processing branches: one for 'ROAD' and another for 'StreetSCENE'. Each branch processes rays extracted from the respective input data. The 'ROAD' branch (top right, enclosed in a blue dashed box) takes road rays with RGB, depth, and normal information as input. These rays are dynamically sampled and processed through a 'Road Radiance Fields' module, visualized as a 3D cube with intersecting rays labeled Ray1, Ray2, Ray3. This module outputs a cost matrix of road rays, which is then processed by a 'Spatial Dynamic Temporal Invariant' block to predict the road point cloud PC_r. Similarly, the 'StreetSCENE' branch (bottom right, enclosed in a red dashed box) processes scene rays with RGB, depth, and normal data through a 'Scene Radiance Fields' module (also visualized with rays intersecting a 3D cube) and a matching 'Spatial Dynamic Temporal Invariant' block to predict the scene point cloud PC_s. Both predicted point clouds, PC_r and PC_s, are merged via a 'Merge' operation to produce the final 'complete street-view point cloud', which is visually represented as a dense 3D point cloud overlaid on a StreetScenes image and highlighted within a yellow dotted box. The merged point cloud includes both road and non-road elements, with the road region explicitly outlined in red. The entire workflow emphasizes separation of road and scene components before merging, leveraging dynamic sampling and radiance field modeling for accurate point cloud reconstruction.

The figure illustrates the detailed architecture of FINO, a multi-stage deep learning framework composed of three main modules: CDL (Compensated Detail Learning), Shape-Aware Module, and REGA (Robust Enhancement and Gating Architecture). The overall layout is vertically segmented into three distinct regions, each enclosed by a dashed border and labeled accordingly.

In the top section, CDL receives two inputs: a coarse feature map C_i (represented as a gray rectangular block) and a higher-resolution feature Z_{i+1} (blue rectangular block). Z_{i+1} is first upsampled via an 'Upsample' operation (gray rounded rectangle), then processed by a '1x1Conv' (beige rounded rectangle). Concurrently, C_i is passed through two parallel '1x1Conv' layers (beige rounded rectangles). The outputs from these three branches are concatenated using a circular 'C' symbol, followed by a '3x3Conv' layer (beige rounded rectangle). The result is passed through a softmax function (text label above arrow) to produce a 3x3 grid of green-toned squares representing a spatial attention or compensation mask. This mask is multiplied element-wise (indicated by a circular '×' symbol) with the output of one of the C_i branches to generate T_i (orange rectangular block).

The middle section, labeled 'Shape-Aware Module', takes T_i (green rectangular block) as input. It splits into multiple parallel branches, each containing a small 3D cube structure with orange and white blocks, representing localized feature processing. These branches converge via concatenation ('C'), followed by a '1x1Conv' layer (light beige rounded rectangle). The output is added (⊕) to another branch originating from T_i, producing H_i (beige rectangular block). A separate path from this addition feeds into an MLP (orange rounded rectangle), which computes a loss term L_sal,i (dark gray rectangular block). Additionally, a black-and-white binary mask with scattered white patches is shown, indicating the learned shape or saliency map derived from this module.

The bottom section, labeled 'REGA', integrates H_i (orange rectangular block) with two temporal feature maps X_t1,i and X_t2,i (gray rectangular blocks). These are combined via concatenation ('C') and passed through a 'Conv' layer (blue rounded rectangle), followed by a sigmoid activation σ (circle with σ symbol). The output is added (⊕) to a mask signal (black-and-white striped bar labeled 'mask'), which is derived from M (black binary mask with white speckles). The resulting gate controls the multiplication (×) of X_t1,i and X_t2,i, producing I_t1,i and I_t2,i respectively. These are then fed into a 'CCL' block (light green rounded rectangle), which generates the final output Z_i (blue rectangular block). The mask M is explicitly shown as a regularization component influencing the gating mechanism, enhancing robustness against pseudo changes.

The figure illustrates the Dual Scale Aggregation (DSA) framework, designed for temporal feature aggregation in video processing. The global layout is left-to-right, starting with five input frames labeled I_{T-2}, I_{T-1}, I_T, I_{T+1}, I_{T+2}, arranged vertically on the far left. These frames depict a silhouette of a person in motion against a textured background, indicating a dynamic scene. A green, vertically oriented hexagonal block labeled 'E' represents an encoder module that processes all five frames simultaneously, producing a set of feature maps for each frame. These feature maps are visualized as grid-like matrices, where each cell corresponds to a spatial location, and colored regions indicate different types of areas: light orange for consistency areas, blue for discrepancy areas, and green for residual areas.

The central part of the diagram shows the dual-scale aggregation process. For each frame's feature map, two types of affinity matrices are computed: short-term (vanilla) affinity W^s and long-term (residual) affinity W^l. The short-term affinity is derived from adjacent frames (e.g., I_{T-1} and I_T), while the long-term affinity is derived from non-adjacent frames (e.g., I_{T-2} and I_T). This is indicated by dashed arrows: red-dotted lines for vanilla affinity (W^s) connecting adjacent frame features, and green-dashed lines for residual affinity (W^l) connecting non-adjacent frame features. Each affinity computation is symbolized by a black circle with a cross, denoting matrix multiplication.

The resulting affinity matrices are then applied to the feature maps via matrix multiplication, producing updated feature representations. The output of these operations is shown as new grid matrices, where the green cells (residual areas) appear in the results of W^l operations, and the orange cells (consistency areas) remain or are enhanced in the results of W^s operations. All these processed feature maps are then fed into a ResBlock (a residual block, depicted as a blue rectangle with rounded corners), which aggregates them into a final output feature map. This aggregated map is shown on the far right, with dark orange and light orange cells representing the aggregated area, indicating the combined result of both short-term and long-term consistency.

A legend at the bottom right clarifies the visual encoding: a black circle with a cross denotes matrix multiplication; blue squares represent discrepancy areas; light orange squares represent consistency areas; green squares represent residual areas; and dark orange squares represent aggregated areas. Additionally, green-dashed arrows indicate residual affinity (W^l), and red-dotted arrows indicate vanilla affinity (W^s). The entire workflow emphasizes leveraging both local (short-term) and global (long-term) temporal relationships to improve feature representation, particularly for handling deformable regions in motion sequences.

The figure illustrates the E2TP (Element-to-Tuple Prediction) framework for aspect-based sentiment analysis, structured into three main stages: First Step: Predicting single elements; Second Step: Mapping predicted elements to their corresponding tuples; and Output Finalization. The global layout is hierarchical and flow-based, starting from an input review at the top, progressing through two parallel processing paths (T1 and T2), and culminating in aggregated output tuples at the bottom. The input review, labeled as x, is a sentence: 'In this Japanese seaside restaurant, the sushi and the view are both perfect, especially in the evening!'.

In the First Step, four separate prediction tasks are performed in parallel, each represented by a light blue rounded rectangle. These tasks ask: what aspects? (answer: sushi, view), what opinions? (answer: perfect, perfect), what categories? (answer: food, location), and what sentiments? (answer: positive, positive). These predictions feed into two distinct processing branches, T1 and T2, indicated by dashed lines and labeled with magenta T1 and T2.

The Second Step is divided into two vertical columns under T1 and T2, each containing six light orange rounded rectangles representing query-answer pairs. In the T1 column, each query targets a specific predicted element (e.g., 'x → sushi') and asks for its associated attributes in a fixed order: aspect, opinion, category, sentiment. The answers provide the full tuple components, e.g., for 'sushi': sushi, perfect, food, positive. In the T2 column, the queries also target individual elements but use a templated format with bracketed role indicators: [A] for aspect, [O] for opinion, [C] for category, [S] for sentiment. The answers fill these slots, e.g., for 'sushi': [A] sushi [O] perfect [C] food [S] positive. Notably, for the word 'perfect', the T2 path includes an additional [SSEP] token, indicating a special handling of shared or overlapping elements. Both T1 and T2 paths conclude with a 'PEP (1st fixed)' step, which stands for Prompt Element Permutation with the first element fixed, as noted in the caption reference to section \ref{sec:pepf}.

The final stage, Output Finalization, involves aggregation. Each branch feeds into an 'Aggregation' box (light orange rounded rectangle), which combines the processed tuples. The outputs from both T1 and T2 aggregations converge to produce the final set of tuples: {(sushi, perfect, food, positive), (view, perfect, location, positive)}, displayed in a light yellow rounded rectangle. The figure uses color-coding to distinguish elements: blue for aspects, red for opinions, green for categories, and purple for sentiments. All text within the boxes is black, except for the colored keywords. The overall structure emphasizes a dual-path approach to robustly map elements to complete tuples before final aggregation.

The figure presents an overview of EFACT’s auto-completion workflow, divided into two main phases: External Func Extraction Phase and External Func Completion Phase. Similarly, the Partially Complete Output in C/C++ Program Format is sent via dashed arrow to other static binary rewriting tools like Lasagne (yellow oval), representing external tools used beyond EFACT’s scope. The figure presents an overview of the Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture, illustrating its end-to-end processing pipeline for image classification. The global layout is divided into two main sections: the left side shows the full ViT model structure, while the right side provides a detailed breakdown of the Transformer Encoder block, separated by a vertical dashed line.

On the left, the process begins at the bottom with an input image, which is divided into a grid of non-overlapping patches. These patches are shown as small image tiles, and are then passed through a 'Linear Projection of Flattened Patches' module, represented as a light pink rectangular box. This step converts each patch into a fixed-dimensional vector. Above this, a sequence of ten embedded tokens (numbered 0* through 9) is displayed, where token 0* is marked as an extra learnable [class] embedding, distinct from the other patch embeddings. These tokens are labeled 'Patch + Position Embedding', indicating that positional information has been added to the flattened patch vectors. All these embeddings are fed into a large gray rectangular block labeled 'Transformer Encoder'.

The output of the Transformer Encoder is connected to an 'MLP Head' (a light orange rectangle), which processes the final representation, particularly the class token (token 0*), to produce a classification result. The output is shown as a rounded orange box listing possible classes such as 'Bird', 'Ball', 'Car', etc., indicating the model's prediction.

On the right, the internal structure of the 'Transformer Encoder' is expanded. It is depicted as a gray box containing a stack of layers repeated L times, indicated by 'L x' at the top. The input to this block is 'Embedded Patches' (light pink rectangle). The first layer is a 'Norm' (yellow rectangle), followed by a 'Multi-Head Attention' module (green rectangle). The output of this attention layer is added to the input via a residual connection (indicated by a circular '+' symbol and a feedback arrow). The result is then passed through another 'Norm' (yellow), followed by an 'MLP' (light blue rectangle). Another residual connection adds the MLP output back to the pre-MLP state, completing one encoder layer. This entire stack is repeated L times, and the final output is passed upward to the next stage in the ViT pipeline.

All connections are represented by solid black arrows, indicating the forward flow of data. The color coding helps distinguish components: pink for input/patch-related modules, yellow for normalization layers, green for attention, blue for MLP, and gray for the main encoder block. The figure effectively abstracts the ViT method as a sequence of patchification, embedding, position encoding, and transformer-based feature learning, culminating in classification via an MLP head.

The figure illustrates the architectural structure of a neural network model designed for sentence-level classification, with a focus on feature-aware attention and interaction mechanisms. The overall layout is vertically organized into a central processing pipeline flanked by detailed expansions of key modules on the left and right sides. The central dashed box contains the main flow: starting from the bottom, an input sentence X = 'they also fly f-16s' is processed through a Feature Engineering Module (green), which extracts atomic features and combines them into complex features. This module feeds into an Encoder Module (gray), which generates contextualized hidden states h₁ through h₈. These hidden states are then passed to a Feature-aware Attention Module (orange), which computes attention weights using two separate attention heads, each receiving linearly transformed inputs from the encoder outputs. The attention outputs AF₁ and AF₂ are combined with a global feature f₀ to produce refined representations.

On the right side, the Sentence Interaction Module (light blue) receives the encoded features and processes them through a Transform Component (gray), followed by Feature Injection (yellow), which maps specific features f₁ to f₈ onto the hidden state sequence via a sparse matrix. This is further enhanced by Convolutional Interaction (blue), consisting of multiple stacked blocks each containing a 1×1 convolution, a 3×3 HDC layer, and a GELU activation, repeated N times. The output of this module feeds back into the Feature-aware Attention Module and ultimately into the Classification Module (light blue) at the top, which produces the final prediction.

The left side provides a detailed breakdown of the Feature-aware Attention Module, showing two parallel attention branches, each with Linear layers feeding into Attention blocks, with f₀ acting as a shared context. Below it, the Feature Engineering Module is expanded to show the process of extracting atomic features from the input and combining them into complex features represented as connected nodes.

The right side includes a visual representation of Feature Injection as a grid where rows correspond to hidden states h₁–h₈ and columns to features f₁–f₈, with highlighted cells indicating which features are injected into which hidden states. The connections between modules are indicated by solid blue arrows, showing the forward flow of information, while feedback loops are shown from the Convolutional Interaction and Feature Injection components back to the Feature-aware Attention Module. The entire diagram uses distinct colors and shapes to differentiate modules: green for feature engineering, gray for encoding, orange for attention, yellow for feature injection, light blue for interaction and classification, and blue for convolutional processing.

The figure presents an overview of the CDDM (Conditional Diffusion Denoising Model) framework for sparse-view CT reconstruction, structured into two main stages: latent space diffusion and pixel space one-step reconstruction. The global layout is left-to-right, beginning with an initial low-resolution CT image x₀^ADMM on the far left, which serves as input to an Image Encoder ε_τ. This encoder maps the image into a latent space, represented by a light blue rectangular region labeled 'Latent Space'. Within this space, a sequence of latent variables l_T, l_{T−τ₁}, ..., l₀ is generated, where l_T follows a standard normal distribution N(0, I), and each subsequent latent variable is processed through a series of blue vertical blocks representing denoising steps in the diffusion process. These latent variables are then decoded back into pixel space to produce a set of noisy, low-quality reconstructions denoted as x̂₀^latent, which are shown as a vertical stack of grayscale CT images. 

From this point, the workflow transitions into the 'Pixel Space' section, enclosed in a large orange rounded rectangle. This stage is divided into two submodules: 'Data consistency' (white dashed box) and 'Discrepancy Mitigation' (pink dashed box). In the 'Data consistency' module, noise is added to each reconstructed image via +ε_K, resulting in a set of noisy images x_K. Each of these is passed through a 'noise predict' step, which outputs a denoised version x̃_0^K. These denoised images are then fed into a 3D ADMM (Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers) block, depicted as a stack of slices with x, y, z axes, indicating that it processes gradients in different spatial directions separately. The ADMM output is a set of reconstructed images x̃_0^recon, which are further refined by adding noise +ε_k to generate intermediate reconstructions x̃_K^recon. 

These intermediate reconstructions are then passed to the 'Discrepancy Mitigation' module, which applies another diffusion process to correct errors introduced during data consistency. The output of this module is a sequence of increasingly refined images, labeled x_{K−T_p}, ..., x₀, culminating in the final high-quality reconstructed CT image. 

Connections between modules are indicated by arrows: from the latent space decoder to the pixel space inputs, from each noisy image to its denoised counterpart, from the denoised images to the ADMM block, and from the ADMM output to the discrepancy mitigation module. A feedback loop from the ADMM block to a green diamond-shaped discriminator D suggests a possible adversarial or consistency check component. The entire process emphasizes iterative refinement using diffusion models in both latent and pixel spaces, with ADMM enforcing data consistency and a secondary diffusion process mitigating discrepancies.

The figure presents an overview of a density-descending feature perturbation strategy for semi-supervised learning, structured into two main phases: (a) Learning Density Distribution and (b) Perturbation Generation. The global layout is divided into two horizontal sections, with (a) at the top in a light beige background and (b) at the bottom in a light green background, indicating distinct operational modes. On the left, unlabeled images are fed into both a teacher and a student network, each with an encoder and decoder. The teacher network uses a moving average of the student’s parameters, denoted by dashed black arrows labeled 'Moving Average'.

In section (a), the teacher encoder processes the input to produce features V, represented as a stack of four cyan squares. These features are passed through a 'Stop Gradient' operation before being fed into a 'Density Estimator' marked with a red flame icon, indicating training mode. This estimator learns a feature density distribution, visualized as a black curve with multiple peaks, using likelihood maximization (denoted by blue arrows) to fit a mixture of Gaussian distributions (shown as cyan dashed curves). The learned latent variables Z, depicted as four green circles, are used to generate pseudo labels via the teacher decoder, followed by label filtering. The pseudo labels are then used to supervise the student model.

In section (b), the student encoder processes the same input to generate features V, also represented as four cyan squares. These features are again passed through a 'Stop Gradient' block and fed into a 'Density Estimator' marked with a blue snowflake icon, indicating evaluation mode. The density estimator computes the density-descending direction, represented by red arrows pointing downward along the feature density distribution, which corresponds to the gradient of the density objective. This gradient, denoted δ*, is combined element-wise (indicated by a plus symbol) with the original features to generate perturbed features, shown as four red-outlined squares. This perturbation injection, labeled T(V), is then fed into the student decoder to produce student predictions. The student predictions are supervised by the pseudo labels from the teacher model via a consistency loss L_ft_con.

The figure includes a legend in the top-left corner: a red flame for Training Mode, a blue snowflake for Evaluation Mode, a red dashed arrow for Gradient Extraction, and a plus sign for Element-wise Sum. The connections between modules are clearly marked: solid black arrows indicate forward passes, dashed black arrows indicate parameter updates (moving average), blue arrows represent likelihood maximization in the teacher phase, and red arrows denote gradient extraction and perturbation flow in the student phase. The entire process leverages weak-to-strong consistency regularization, where the teacher generates reliable pseudo labels, and the student learns to predict them under density-descending perturbations.

The figure presents the training scheme and overall architecture of the I2I-Galip model for image-to-image translation between medical imaging domains, specifically focusing on translating from domain B to domain A (e.g., T1-weighted to T2-weighted MRI). The diagram is divided into three parts: (a), (b), and (c), each illustrating different components of the loss functions and network structure.

Part (a) outlines the core architecture. On the left, an input image X_B from domain B is fed into a U-Net generator. Simultaneously, a text prompt 'This MRI image is T2-Weighted' (denoted as T_A) is processed by a CLIP Text Encoder (a purple rounded rectangle). The encoded text features are injected into multiple levels of the U-Net via skip connections, guiding the generation process. The U-Net outputs a translated image, which is then passed through a CLIP ViT-B encoder (a light green stacked block with red CLS tokens at the start of each layer) to extract visual features. These features are fed into a discriminator head (Head_A, a blue circle) to compute adversarial loss L_adv. Additionally, the generated image’s features are compared with those of the target image X_A (from domain A) using another CLIP ViT-B encoder to compute classification loss L_cls. The CLIP ViT-B encoder also computes the CLIP loss L_clip by aligning the generated image features with the text embedding from T_A. All CLIP components (ViT-B and Text Encoder) have frozen parameters during training.

Part (b) illustrates the cycle consistency loss L_cycle. Here, the translated image from X_B using T_A is further translated back to domain B using a second U-Net guided by text T_B (e.g., 'This MRI image is T1-Weighted'). The final output is compared with the original X_B to enforce cycle consistency, ensuring the translation is reversible and preserves content.

Part (c) shows the identity loss L_identity. In this setup, an image X_B is translated using text T_B (same domain) and should ideally remain unchanged. The output is compared with the original X_B to ensure the model does not alter images when translating within the same domain.

The U-Net modules are depicted as light green encoders with skip connections (dotted lines) and upsample paths (solid arrows). The CLIP Text Encoder is consistently shown as a purple rounded rectangle. CLIP ViT-B is represented as a vertical stack of layers, each containing a red CLS token followed by multiple white boxes representing feature tokens. Losses are labeled with bold text (L_adv, L_cls, L_clip, L_cycle, L_identity) and connected via dotted lines to indicate their computational dependencies. The figure uses black-and-white MRI brain slices as input/output examples, with X_B and X_A denoting source and target domain images, respectively.

The figure illustrates the network architecture of ResCBAM, a variant of the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) integrated with a residual block structure. The overall layout is a horizontal flow from left to right, beginning with an 'Input Feature' module and ending with an 'Output Feature' module, both represented as rounded rectangles with a light purple fill. The core of the architecture consists of two sequential attention modules: C-Attention (Channel Attention) and S-Attention (Spatial Attention), each enclosed in a distinct colored background—C-Attention in light peach and S-Attention in light blue—to visually separate their functional components.

In the C-Attention module, the input feature is split into two parallel paths: one passes through a 'Global Average Pooling' block (light brown rectangle), and the other through a 'Global Max Pooling' block (light red rectangle). Both pooled outputs are fed into a shared 'Multi-Layer Perceptron' (gray vertical rectangle), which processes them. The outputs from the MLP are then element-wise added using a circular plus symbol, followed by a 'Sigmoid' activation function (light green rectangle). This sigmoid output is multiplied element-wise (indicated by a circular multiplication symbol) with the original input feature, producing the 'Channel Refined Feature' (light green rounded rectangle).

This channel-refined feature is then passed to the S-Attention module. Here, the same dual pooling strategy is applied: 'Global Average Pooling' and 'Global Max Pooling' (same color coding as before). Their outputs are concatenated using a circular 'C' symbol, forming a combined feature map. This is processed by a '7x7 Convolution' layer (yellow rectangle), followed by a 'Sigmoid' activation (light green rectangle). The resulting spatial attention map is then multiplied element-wise with the channel-refined feature, yielding the 'Final Refined Feature' (light green rounded rectangle).

Finally, the final refined feature is added to the original input feature via a circular plus symbol, implementing the residual connection characteristic of ResNet-style architectures. This sum produces the 'Output Feature', completing the forward pass. The diagram uses solid black arrows to indicate data flow between modules, with clear directional connections showing how features propagate through the attention mechanisms and residual connection. All text labels are centered within their respective blocks, and the visual hierarchy emphasizes the modular design of CBAM enhanced with residual learning.
